﴿Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an.﴾ Before the commentary, we say: concerning the surah there are several matters.
The first: this surah is recited in the Eid prayer, because of His words in it, exalted is He: ﴿That is the Day of Coming Forth﴾ [Qaf: 42], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿Such is the coming forth﴾ [Qaf: 11], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿That is a easy gathering for Us﴾ [Qaf: 44]. The Eid is a day of adornment, so a person should not forget his coming forth to the grounds of reckoning, nor be exultant and boastful on that day, nor commit wickedness or sin. When God commanded the Prophet ﷺ to remind, by His words at the end of the surah: ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾ [Qaf: 45], He reminded them of what suits their state on their day by His words: ﴿Qaf. By the Qur'an.﴾
The second: this surah and the surah "Sad" share in beginning with the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-mu'jama), the oath by the Qur'an, His words ﴿Nay﴾ [Qaf: 2], and the expression of wonder. They share something else: the beginning and end of the two surahs correspond. In "Sad," He said at its beginning: ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ [Sad: 1], and at its end: ﴿It is only a reminder to the worlds﴾ [Sad: 87]. In "Qaf," He said at its beginning: ﴿By the glorious Qur'an,﴾ and at its end: ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾ [Qaf: 45]. Thus it opens with what it closes with.
The third: in that surah (Sad) the focus is on establishing the first principle, which is tawhid, by His words: ﴿Has he made the gods one God?﴾ [Sad: 5] and His words: ﴿Go on, and be steadfast for your gods﴾ [Sad: 6]. In this surah (Qaf) the focus is on establishing the other principle, which is resurrection, by His words: ﴿When we are dead and turned to dust—that is a far return﴾ [Qaf: 3]. Since the opening of Sad was establishing the origin, He closed it with: ﴿When your Lord said to the angels, "I am creating a human from clay"﴾

[Sad: 71] and concluded it with the account of the beginning of the creation of Adam, because that is evidence of the Oneness. Since the opening of this one (Qaf) is to explain resurrection, He closed it with: ﴿On the Day the earth splits asunder from them, hastening. That is a easy gathering for Us﴾ [Qaf: 44].

As for the interpretation, it contains several issues:

The first issue: it has been said that ﴿Qaf﴾ is the name of a mountain surrounding the world. It has also been said that its meaning is wisdom, which is our saying: "the matter has been decided." In "Sad" (it means): God has spoken the truth. We have already mentioned that the letters are alerts placed before the Qur'an, so that the listener remains attentive to what comes to him, and nothing of the splendid speech and the exceptional meaning escapes him.

We have also mentioned that worship is of several kinds: some is of the heart, some of the tongue, and some is outward and apparent. Among the bodily acts, some have a meaning that is understood, and some have a meaning that is not understood, such as the rites of the Hajj like stoning and running (between Safa and Marwa) and others. Among the acts of the heart, some are understood through evidence, such as the knowledge of tawhid, the possibility of resurrection, the attributes of God exalted, and the truthfulness of the Messengers. And among them are matters that remove them from being understood in meaning: matters that cannot be affirmed and firmly believed except through revelation, such as the Path (sirat) stretched over Hell, sharper than the sword and finer than a hair, and the Balance by which deeds are weighed. Likewise, the remembrances which are the verbal worship should be of the same kind: some whose meaning is understood, like nearly the entire Qur'an except a little of it, and some that are not understood or comprehended, like the disjointed letters, because pronouncing them is pure submission to the command, not for what there is in speech of the beauty of narration or the aim at a purpose, such as our saying: "Forgive us and have mercy on us" [al-Baqara: 286]. Rather, uttering them is purely an act of devotion. Another consideration supports this: these letters are used as oaths. When God swore by the fig and the olive, it was an honouring of them; so when He swears by the letters, which are the basis of noble speech, which is the proof of knowledge and the instrument of definition, it is more fitting. Having understood this, we say that on this there are discussions:

The first: God's oath has occurred with one thing, as in His words: ﴿By the time﴾ [al-Asr: 1] and His words: ﴿By the star﴾ [al-Najm: 1]; and with one letter, as in His words: ﴿Sad﴾ and ﴿Nun﴾. It has occurred with two things, as in His words: ﴿By the morning brightness, and by the night when it is still﴾ [al-Duha: 1] and His words: ﴿By the sky and the night-comer﴾ [al-Tariq: 1]; and with two letters, as in ﴿Ta Ha﴾, ﴿Ta Sin﴾, ﴿Ya Sin﴾, and ﴿Ha Mim﴾; and with three things, as in His words: ﴿By those who range in ranks﴾, ﴿by those who drive with a driving﴾, ﴿by those who recite﴾; and with three letters, as in ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾, ﴿Ta Sin Mim﴾, and ﴿Alif Lam Ra﴾; and with four things, as in ﴿By the scatterers﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 1], ﴿By the sky of the constellations﴾ [al-Buruj: 1], and ﴿By the fig﴾ [al-Tin: 1]; and with four letters, as in ﴿Alif Lam Mim Sad﴾ and ﴿Alif Lam Mim Ra﴾; and with five things, as in ﴿By the Mount﴾ [al-Tur: 1], ﴿By those sent forth﴾ [al-Mursalat: 1], ﴿By those who pull out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 1], and ﴿By the dawn﴾ [al-Fajr: 1]; and with five letters, as in ﴿Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad﴾, ﴿Ha Mim﴾, ﴿Ayn Sin Qaf﴾. He has not sworn by more than five things except in one surah, which is ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [al-Shams: 1]. He has not sworn by more than five roots, because it gathers a word of heaviness; and since it is heavy when composed for a meaning, its heaviness when composed without comprehension of the meaning, or without any meaning, is even greater.

The second discussion: when swearing by known things, He mentioned the particle of oath, which is the waw, and said: ﴿By the Mount﴾, ﴿By the star﴾, ﴿By the sun﴾. But when swearing by letters, He did not mention the particle of oath, so He did not say "and Qaf" or "and Ha Mim," because since the oath was by the letters themselves, the letter was itself the thing sworn by. So He did not bring it in the place where it would be the instrument of the oath, establishing equality between the letters.

The third discussion: God swore by things such as the fig and the Mount, and did not swear by their roots, which are the simple substances, water and earth. He swore by letters without composition, because things, in His sight, He composes in their best state. As for letters: if they are composed with a meaning, the oath falls on the meaning and not on the utterance, as in our saying: ﴿By the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-Anbiya: 16]. If they are composed without meaning, the single letter is more noble, so He swore by the individual letters.

The fourth discussion: He swore by letters at the beginning of twenty-eight surahs, and by things whose number equals the number of letters, excluding ﴿By the sun﴾ [al-Shams: 1], in fourteen surahs. This is because the oath by things, other than letters, occurred at the beginnings of surahs and within them, as in His words: ﴿Nay, by the moon, and by the night when it withdraws﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 33], His words: ﴿And by the night and what it gathers﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 17], and His words: ﴿By the night when it turns its back﴾ [al-Takwir: 17]. The oath by letters is not found, and is not appropriate, except at the beginnings of surahs, because mentioning what is not understood in meaning within the flow of an ordered, understood speech disrupts understanding. Since the oath by things has two places, and the oath by letters has one place, the oath by things at the beginnings of surahs was made half of the oath by letters at their beginnings.

The fifth discussion: the oath by letters occurs in both halves, indeed in every seven, while the oath by enumerated things is found only in the second half, indeed only in the last seven, except for "those who range in ranks." This is because we have explained that the oath by letters is almost always accompanied by mention of the Qur'an, the Book, or the Revelation after it, as in: ﴿Ya Sin. By the wise Qur'an﴾ [Ya Sin: 1-2]; ﴿Ha Mim. The revelation of the Book﴾ [Ghafir: 1-2]; ﴿Alif Lam Mim. That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqara: 1-2]. Since the entire Qur'an is a miracle conveyed by letters, this was found generally in all places, and this is not the case with the oath by enumerated things. We have mentioned some of this in the commentary on Surah al-Ankabut.

Let us mention what is specific to Qaf. It has been said that it is the name of a mountain surrounding the earth, upon which are the extremities of the sky. This is weak for several reasons:

One: the most common reading is to pause on it. If it were the name of a mountain, pausing would not be permitted in continuous recitation, because whoever says that would hold that God swore by it.

Two: if it were so, it would have been mentioned with the particle of oath, as in His words: ﴿By the Mount﴾ [al-Tur: 1]. This is because the particle of oath is omitted where the thing sworn by deserves to be sworn by, as when we say: "By God, I will do such-and-such," and that it deserves this is clear without indication by the word. It is not good to say: "Zayd, I will surely do it."

Three: if it were as he mentioned, it would be written as qaf with alif and fa, as ﴿a spring of running water﴾ [al-Ghashiya: 12] is written, and as ﴿Is not God sufficient for His servant?﴾ [al-Zumar: 36] is written. But in all the mushafs the letter ﴿Qaf﴾ is written as it is.

Four: the apparent matter is that its case is like that of ﴿Sad﴾, ﴿Nun﴾, and ﴿Ha Mim﴾, which are letters, not words. Likewise ﴿Qaf﴾. If it is said that this is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, we say: what is transmitted from him is that "Qaf" is the name of a mountain, but that this is what is meant in this place, no. It has also been said that its meaning is "the matter has been decided," and in "Sad," "God has spoken the truth." It has also been said that it is the active participle of qafa yaqfu, and "Sad" from sada, from al-musadah, which is opposition. The meaning is: this is one who traces (qafin) all things by uncovering them, and its meaning then is His words: ﴿Nor is any moist or dry thing, but it is in a clear Book﴾ [al-An'am: 59], if we say that the Book there is the Qur'an. This is what has been said about Qaf.

As for its recitation, there are many readings, and to restrict them one must explain their meanings. We say: if we say it is indeclinable on what we have explained, then its proper form is pausing, since it has no governing agent, and so it resembles the building of sounds. Kasra is permitted to avoid meeting two unvocalized letters, and fatha is permitted by preferring the lighter. If it is asked: how is choosing fatha permitted here, when it is not permitted when two unvocalized letters meet, one being the last word and the other the first of another word, as in His words: ﴿Those who disbelieved did not﴾ [al-Bayyina: 1] and ﴿And do not drive away those who﴾ [al-An'am: 52]? We say: because there, the vowelling was required, and kasra was specified for the verb, due to the resemblance to inflectional movement, since the verb is a position where raf' and nasb may occur but jarr does not occur in it. So kasra was chosen, which no one would mistake for jarr, since a verb does not take jarr; and if it were fathah it would be confused with nasb. But at the ends of nouns there is no confusion, since nouns are positions where the three vowels occur, so avoidance was not possible, and they chose the lighter.

If we say they are a letter sworn by, then their proper form is jarr. Nasb is permitted by making it an object of "aqsama" in the manner of connection, with the preposition considered as if absent. If we say they are the name of the surah, and if we say it is sworn by in addition, then its proper form is fatha, since it is then not declined, so it is fathah in a position of jarr, as you say "wa Ibrahima and Ahmada" when swearing by them. If we say it is not sworn by and say it is the name of the surah, then its proper form is raf' if we take it as a predicate, its estimate being: "this is Qaf." If we say it is from qafa yaqfu, then its proper form is tanwin, as when we say "hadha da'in wa ra'in." If we say it is the name of a mountain, then it is jarr and tanwin, even if it is an oath.

Now let us return to the interpretation. We say: the adjective (*wasf*) may be used for distinction (*tamyiz*), which is the more common usage, as when we say "the eternal speech" (*al-kalam al-qadim*) to distinguish it from the created, or "the noble man" (*al-rajul al-karim*) to distinguish him from the base. It may also be used merely for praise, as when we say "God, the Generous" (*Allah al-Karim*), since there is no other god in existence from whom we would need to distinguish Him by "the Generous." In this place, both possibilities are admissible, but the apparent meaning is that it is merely for praise. As for distinction, it would be by making the Qur'an a name for "that which is recited" (*al-maqru'*). This is indicated by God's words: ﴿Had there been a Qur'an by which the mountains could be moved...﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:31]. As for *al-majid* (the glorious), it is "the great" (*al-'azim*). It was also said that *al-majid* means one of abundant generosity (*kathir al-karam*). On both interpretations the Qur'an is *majid*. On our statement that *al-majid* is "the great," this is because the Qur'an is of great benefit, because it is the remembrance of the great God, and the remembrance of the great is great, and because no one among creation has been able to produce its like. It is a sign of greatness; one says "a great king" when he cannot be overcome. This is indicated by God's words: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] and the great Qur'an﴾ [al-Hijr 15:87], meaning the one that no one can match, so that it would be a miracle (*mu'jizah*) indicating your prophethood. And His words: ﴿Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an, [inscribed] in a preserved tablet﴾ [al-Buruj 85:21–22], meaning preserved from being perceived by anyone except by God's making it known, so it is not altered or changed; and ﴿falsehood cannot approach it from before it or behind it﴾ [Fussilat 41:42]. Thus it is not within anyone's power to produce, and so it is great. As for our statement that *al-majid* is "one of abundant generosity," the Qur'an is generous: whoever seeks his aim from it finds it, and it enriches everyone who takes refuge in it, and enriching the needy is the utmost generosity. This is indicated by the fact that *al-majid* is paired with *al-hamid* (the praiseworthy) in our saying: "Indeed You are praiseworthy and glorious" (*innaka hamidun majid*). *Al-hamid* is the one who is thanked, and thanks are for a favour, and the benefactor is generous. So *al-majid* is the one who is generous to the utmost degree.

There are, in this, several discussions:

The first: The Qur'an is that by which an oath (*qasam*) is sworn, so what is the thing sworn to? We say: there are several views on this, and their classification is that we say: this is either understood from a contextual indication (*qarinah haliyyah*) or a verbal indication (*qarinah maqaliyyah*). The verbal indication is either prior to the thing sworn by or subsequent to it. If we say that it is understood from a prior verbal indication, then there is nothing prior to it in wording except *Qaf*, so the construction would be: "This is Qaf, and by the Qur'an, the glorious," or "Qaf: God sent it down," with ﴿and the Qur'an﴾ following, just as one says "This is Hatim, by God," meaning he is the one famous for generosity; and one says "I saw the crescent moon, by God." If we say it is understood from a subsequent verbal indication, we say: that refers to two matters: the first is *al-mundhir* (the warner), and the second is *al-raj'* (the return). So the construction would be: "By the glorious Qur'an, you are indeed the warner," or "By the glorious Qur'an, the return is certainly to come," because both matters are explicitly the subject of the oath. As for the first, it is indicated by God's words: ﴿Ya Sin. By the wise Qur'an, indeed you are among the messengers﴾ [Ya Sin 36:1–3], up to His saying: ﴿that you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned﴾ [Ya Sin 36:6]. As for the second, it is indicated by God's words: ﴿By the Mount, and by a Book inscribed, [in a parchment unfolded]...﴾ [al-Tur 52:1–2], up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is to occur﴾ [al-Tur 52:7–8]. This second view becomes most evident on the opinion of the one who said that *Qaf* is the name of a mountain, since the oath would then be by the mountain and the Qur'an, and there the oath is by "the Tur" and "the inscribed Book," which are the mountain and the Qur'an. If it is asked: which of these two is more apparent to you? I say: the first, because "warner" is closer to the context than "return," and because we find the letters mentioned alongside the Qur'an, and the matter sworn to is his being a messenger and a warner, whereas we have not found the letters mentioned followed by the gathering (*al-hashr*). Consider this in a sura of them: God's words: ﴿Alif Lam Mim. The revelation of the Book, in which there is no doubt, is from the Lord of the worlds. Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Rather, it is the truth from your Lord, that you may warn﴾ [al-Sajdah 32:1–3]. Also, because the Qur'an is a miracle indicating that Muhammad (ﷺ) is the Messenger of God, so swearing by it, in that sense, is a pointer to the evidence concerning the manner of the oath, and it is not itself evidence for the gathering. Rather, it contains indications which yield certainty about the gathering after knowing the truthfulness of the Messenger. As for if we say it is understood from a contextual indication, then it is that Muhammad (ﷺ) is upon the truth, and his speech has the attribute of truthfulness, since the disbelievers used to deny this. The preferred view is what we have mentioned.

The second: "Rather, they marvel" (*bal 'ajibu*) requires that there be something from which one turns away (*mudrab 'anhu*). What is that? We say: al-Wahidi said, and al-Zamakhshari agreed with him, that it is an implied statement: "What is the matter?", as they say. We will clarify this further. On what we have chosen, the implied construction, God knows best, is: "Qaf. By the glorious Qur'an, indeed you are a warner." It is as if He said after it: "And they doubted it, so turn away from that."

And He says: ﴿Rather, they wonder that a warner has come to them.﴾

That is, they were not content with merely doubting the truth of the matter and setting it aside as possible. Rather, they were certain of its opposite, and they regarded it as one of the strange things.

If it is asked: what is the wisdom in this great abbreviation, in one place, where the thing sworn to and the thing turned away from are both omitted, and the verse gives something that cannot be understood except after great reflection, and cannot be understood with that reflection except by a mighty divine grant of success?

We say: the sworn-to matter was omitted because omitting it, in some contexts, conveys a manifestness that mentioning it does not. For whoever mentions a great king in an assembly and praises him has honoured him. If another then says to him, "He is not mentioned in this assembly," then by directing him to leave off the mention, that person indicates the king's greatness beyond what the speaker gains by mentioning him. So God, exalted is He, says, in effect: your mission is too manifest to need mention.

As for the omission of the thing turned away from (al-muḍrab ʿanhu), it is because when the thing turned away from is mentioned and then turned away from in favour of another matter, this is only fine if there is some gap between the two mentioned things. When the gap is great, it is not fine to mention both with the turning away (al-iḍrāb). An example: it is fine to say, "The vizier honours so-and-so, rather the king honours him." But it is not fine to say, "The doorkeeper honours so-and-so, rather the king honours him," because the distance between them is great. The iḍrāb (turning from one thing to another, "rather") is for gradation. So when the speaker leaves out the thing turned away from explicitly and uses the particle of iḍrāb, two things are gained from it. The first: it points to another matter before it. The second: it makes the second matter a great gap, of the kind that is not mentioned. Here it is likewise, because doubt after the establishment of proof is remote, while certainty in its opposite is at the furthest extreme of remoteness.

**The third discussion:** The verb with *an* (that) operates in the position of a verbal noun (maṣdar). You say, "I was commanded that I should stand," and "I was commanded with standing," and you say, "His answer was only that he said," and "His answer was only his saying such and such." Since this is so, the construction does not depart from the verbal noun, in that it is permissible to say, "I was commanded that I stand," without the particle of attachment (ḥarf al-ilṣāq). It is not permissible to say, "I was commanded the standing," but the particle must be present. For this reason they said, that is, "they wondered at his coming." We say: ﴿that he came to them﴾. Although in meaning it stands in place of the verbal noun, in form it is a verb plus a particle. All particles of transitivity (ḥurūf al-taʿdiyah) are prepositions, and a preposition does not enter upon a verb. So the rule would require that it not enter, and at the least it is permissible that it not enter. Thus it is permissible to say, ﴿they wondered that he came to them﴾, and it is not permissible to say "their coming," because there is no obstacle to the particles entering upon it.

God's saying ﴿from among them﴾ may be taken as a statement confirming their wonder, and it may be taken as a statement negating their wonder. As for confirmation: they used to say, ﴿Shall we follow a single human being from among us?﴾ [al-Qamar 24], and ﴿You are only human beings like us﴾ [Yasin 15], indicating that it is not possible that you be singled out for this lofty station while we share with you in reality and its necessary attributes. As for negation: since he was one of them, seen among them, and what all of them and those after them were unable to do became manifest through him, it would have been obligatory for them to say, "This is not from him, nor from anyone of our kind, so it is from God." This is unlike the case in which a single person from outside their kind came to them and did what they were unable to do. For they would then say, "We cannot, because every species has a distinctive property. The distinctive property of the ostrich is swallowing fire, and of birds is flight in the air, and the son of Adam cannot do it." If it is objected: the negation is permissible, because their saying was false; but how is it permissible to confirm falsehood? We answer: whoever clarifies the falsity of a statement must present it in the most eloquent form possible, and mention in it everything that may be imagined as evidence for it, and then refute it. For this reason He said, "You wonder because he is one of you," while in reality that is the cause of this wonder. If it is objected: the Prophet ﷺ was a bringer of good news and a warner, and God, in all places, puts his being a bringer of good news before his being a warner, so why did He not say, "They wondered that a bringer of good news from among them came to them"? We answer: since he was not specified for the good news in a place, he was for them a warner and nothing else.

Then God, exalted is He, says: ﴿So the disbelievers said, "This is a strange thing."﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: this is another wonder, at another matter, namely the gathering (al-ḥashr), to which He pointed with His saying: ﴿"When we have died and become dust, that is a far return."﴾ [Qaf 3]. So they wondered at his being a warner of the occurrence of the gathering. What indicates this is a consideration of the beginning of Surat Sad, where He says: ﴿They wondered that a warner came to them﴾ and He says: ﴿"Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed this is a strange thing (ʿujāb)."﴾ [Sad 5]. He mentioned their wonder at two matters. The apparent meaning is that their saying ﴿This is a strange thing﴾ refers to the coming of the warner, not to the gathering. Several things indicate this. The first: there, He mentioned ﴿Indeed this is a strange thing﴾ after an interrogative of denial, saying, ﴿"Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed this is a strange thing."﴾ Here He says ﴿This is a strange thing﴾, and what the indicator refers to could only be the coming of the warner.

Then they said, ﴿"When we have died and become dust, that is a far return."﴾ The second: here, after the expression of remoteness by interrogation, there occurs a matter conveying the meaning of wonder, namely their saying ﴿That is a far return﴾, for that is an expression of remoteness, which is like wonder. So if wonder also referred to it, it would be like repetition. If it is objected: an explicit repetition would follow from taking your saying ﴿This is a strange thing﴾ as referring to the coming of the warner, for their wonder at it is already known from His saying ﴿They wondered that he came to them﴾, so ﴿This is a strange thing﴾ would be a repetition. We say: that is not a repetition but a confirmation. This is because when He said ﴿Rather they wondered﴾ in the verbal form, it was also permissible for a person to wonder at what is not strange, as God says: ﴿Do you wonder at the command of God?﴾ [Hud 73], and it is said in common usage: "There is no reason for your wonder at what is not a wonder." So when they wondered, it was said to them: there is no sense in your action and your wonder. They said: ﴿This is a strange thing﴾, so how should we not wonder at it? Another indication of this is that God, exalted is He, said here ﴿So the disbelievers said﴾ with the particle fa' (so), and He said in Sad: ﴿And the disbelievers said, "This is a lying sorcerer."﴾ [Sad 4], because their saying ﴿a lying sorcerer﴾ was obstinacy, not consequent upon what preceded, whereas ﴿This is a strange thing﴾ is a matter consequent upon what preceded, that is, they wondered and denied it, so they said ﴿This is a strange thing﴾, so how should we not wonder at it? Another indication is His saying ﴿That is a far return﴾ with the demonstrative for remoteness, whereas "this" (hādhā) is for what is near and present. So what is indicated by "that" should be other than what is indicated by "this." That is not valid except on our view.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*, *The Keys to the Unseen*) on surah 50, verses 3–4:

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿When we have died and become dust? That is a far return.﴾

When they showed wonder at his messengership, they showed their rejection of his speech. This is like what God, exalted is He, said about them: ﴿They said, "This is only a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship"﴾ [Saba: 43], and ﴿They said, "This is nothing but a fabricated lie"﴾ [Saba: 43]. There are several issues here.

The first issue: His saying ﴿When we have died and become dust?﴾ is a denial by them, either in words or by implication, indicated by His saying ﴿there has come to them a warner﴾. For since the warning was only about a lasting punishment and a painful retribution, it contained an allusion to the Gathering (*hashr*), so they said, ﴿When we have died and become dust?﴾

The second issue: ﴿That﴾ refers to what he said, which is the warning. His saying ﴿This is a strange thing﴾ refers to the coming, as we have said. Since the two descriptions differ, we say: the coming and the one who comes are each present. As for the warning, although it is present, because the thing warned of was not present, they said this about it. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 50, verses 5–8:**

Regarding His saying, ﴿When it came to them﴾, there are two interpretations of the one who came.

The first: it refers to the denier. The sense is: they denied the truth when the truth came to them, meaning they did not delay it for reflection and contemplation.

The second: the one who came here is the one who came in His saying, ﴿Rather, they wondered that a warner from among themselves came to them﴾. The sense is: they denied the truth when the warner came to them. The first interpretation is not valid according to our view that the truth is the Return (al-rajʿ), because they did not deny it at the time it came. Rather, they say, ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52].

As for His saying, ﴿So they are in a confused matter﴾, that is: in a matter that is varied and mixed. Al-Zajjaj and others said: because at one time they say, "He is a sorcerer," at another, "He is a poet," at another they attribute to him soothsaying, and at another, madness. The more correct view is that this explains the disagreement mentioned in the verses. That is because His saying, ﴿Rather, they wondered﴾, indicates a prior matter which was turned away from. We have mentioned that it is doubt, and the sense is: "By the glorious Qur'an, you are indeed a warner, and they doubted you. Rather, they wondered. Rather, they denied." These are three levels: the first is doubt; above it is wonder, because the doubter regards both matters as equal, while the one who wonders has a preponderant belief that the wondrous thing does not occur, but he does not affirm it with certainty; and the denier is one who firmly decides the opposite. So they were doubting, then became suspicious, then became firmly convinced. Then He said, ﴿So they are in a confused matter﴾. The particle fa' (ف) in His saying "fahum" (so they) indicates this, because then their being ﴿in a confused matter﴾ becomes consequent upon what preceded it, whereas on what they [the opponents] claimed, it would not be consequent.

If it is said: the *marij* is the mixed, and these are distinct matters arranged according to the dictates of reason, because the doubter reaches the level of suspicion, the suspicious reaches the level of certainty, and at certainty suspicion does not remain, and at suspicion doubt does not remain. But as for what they claimed, in it mixing occurs, because they had no order in this matter. Rather, at one time they would say, "A soothsayer," and at another, "Mad," and then they would return to attributing him to soothsaying after attributing him to madness, and likewise to poetry after sorcery, and to sorcery after poetry. This is the *marij*.

We say: it was obligatory that they should move from doubt to suspicion of his truthfulness, because of their knowledge of his trustworthiness and his avoidance of lying throughout his life among them; and from suspicion to certainty of his truthfulness, because of the manifest overpowering miracles upon his hands and tongue. But when they reversed the order, the confusion (*maraj*) occurred in it, and the falling into error (*darak*) occurred along with the confusion. As for what they claimed, the fitting interpretation of it is His saying, ﴿Indeed, you are in a varied saying﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 8], because what proceeded from them concerning him was a varied saying. As for doubt, suspicion, and certainty, these are different matters. In this there is a subtle point: the application of the word *marij* to their suspicion and certainty indicates that this certainty was not sound, because sound certainty does not change, whereas for them change was necessary. So their matter was unsettled, unlike the believer who is granted success, for in his belief no hesitation occurs, and no multiplicity is found in his creed.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We built it and adorned it, and it has no rifts?﴾

This is a reference to the proof that refutes their saying: ﴿That is a far-off return﴾. This is like His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 81], and His saying: ﴿Certainly the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir: 57], and His saying: ﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead? Yes﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 33]. There are questions concerning this:

**The first question:** The interrogative hamza (ʾa-) sometimes enters a statement without a waw in it, and sometimes enters it with a waw after it. Is there a difference between the two situations?

We say: there is a difference more subtle than what is apparent. It is that a speaker says: *ʾa-Zaydun fi al-dār baʿdu wa-qad ṭalaʿat al-shams?* (Is Zayd still in the house, and the sun has risen?), mentioning it as a denial. But when he says: *ʾa-wa-Zaydan fi al-dār baʿdu wa-qad ṭalaʿat al-shams?* (And is Zayd still in the house, and the sun has risen?), he indicates by the waw a subtle allusion that the ugliness of his action has become like two ugly actions. It is as if he says, after hearing from someone who had said about Zayd that he is in the house: "Is he heedless while he is still in the house?" Because the waw indicates a sense of a matter different from what follows it, even if there was no prior mention; but by the waw he alludes to it to add to the denial.

If it is said: In one place He said ﴿Have they not looked?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 185], and here He said ﴿So have they not looked?﴾ with the fa' (ف). What is the difference?

We say: here, a denial of the return had preceded from them, so He used the particle of consequence (fa') with its opposite. If it is said: in Ya-Sin, this had preceded with His saying: ﴿He said, "Who will give life to bones?"﴾ [Ya-Sin: 78]? We say: there, the reasoning from the heavens came, because when the denial did not follow the denial, He reasoned with another proof, which is His saying: ﴿Say: He who produced them the first time will give them life﴾ [Ya-Sin: 79], then He mentioned the other proof. Here, the proof came right after the denial, so it was mentioned with the fa'.

As for His saying here with the word "looking" (*naẓar*), and in al-Ahqaf with the word "seeing" (*ruʾya*), there is a subtle point in it: here, when they considered the matter of the return remote by saying ﴿That is a far-off return﴾, He considered their considering it remote as remote, and said: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky?﴾ because looking is less than seeing. So it is as if looking was enough for attaining knowledge of the denial of the return, and there is no need for seeing, so that the remoteness would correspond to remoteness. Whereas there, no denial had been explicitly mentioned from them, so He guided them to it with seeing, which is more complete than looking. Then He perfected and beautified that by His saying: ﴿at the sky﴾ (ilā al-samāʾ), and did not say ﴿in the sky﴾ (fī al-samāʾ), because looking *in* a thing indicates contemplation and intensity, while looking *at* a thing indicates reaching it, since *ilā* denotes the limit (ghāya). So the look ends at it, entering into the sense of a container. When the look has reached it, it should penetrate it so that the sense of being contained is valid.

His saying: ﴿above them﴾ (fawqahum) is another emphasis, that is, it is manifest above their heads, not absent from them.

His saying: ﴿how We built it and adorned it, and it has no rifts﴾ points to the aspect of the proof and the greater likelihood of its occurrence, which is for the return. As for the aspect of the proof: the human being has a foundation, namely the bones, which are like a pillar, and powers and lights like hearing and sight. So the building of the sky is higher than the foundation of the body, and the adornment of the sky is more perfect than the adornment of a human with flesh and fat. As for the greater likelihood: the sky has no rifts, so its composition is stronger, whereas the human has openings and pores. There is no doubt that a stronger composition is like a tightly woven fabric, and a weaker composition is like a loosely woven fabric. The first is more difficult and more wondrous to people. So how do they consider the lesser remote while they know the existence of the higher from Allah, the Exalted?

The philosophers said: the verse indicates that the sky does not accept splitting. They said the same about His saying: ﴿Do you see any flaw?﴾ [al-Mulk: 3] and His saying: ﴿seven strong ones﴾ [al-Naba: 12], and they strained [the meaning] in this, because His saying: ﴿and it has no rifts﴾ is explicit in the negation of that. And reporting the absence of a thing is not reporting the absence of its possibility, for whoever says, "Such-and-such has no omen (*fāl*)," does not indicate the negation of its possibility. Then the Exalted explained the opposite of their claim with His saying: ﴿And when the sky is split open﴾ [al-Mursalat: 9], and He said: ﴿When the sky is cleft asunder﴾ [al-Infitar: 1], and He said: ﴿Then it will be on that day frail﴾ [al-Haqqa: 16], in opposition to His saying: ﴿seven strong ones﴾ [al-Naba: 12], and He said: ﴿And when the sky is split apart and becomes red like oil﴾ [al-Rahman: 37], and other [verses]. All of these are explicit in refuting them. What they claimed as indication is not apparent, nor does it have even a hidden indication. As for their rational proof, it is weaker and more feeble than their reliance on transmitted texts.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And the earth — We spread it out and cast into it firm mountains and caused to grow in it of every beautiful kind of pair﴾.

This is a reference to another proof. The aspect of the earth's indication is that they said: when a human dies and the nutritive and growing faculty departs from him, that faculty does not return to him. We say: the earth is harder in its stillness and more extinguished, yet Allah, the Exalted, causes various kinds of plants to grow in it, and they grow and increase. Likewise, life returns to the human being.

He mentioned three matters concerning the earth, just as He mentioned three matters concerning the sky. For the earth: spreading out, casting in firm mountains, and causing growth in it. For the sky: building, adornment, and closing its rifts. Each one corresponds to one of the other. Spreading out corresponds to building, because spreading is placement (waḍʿ) and building is elevation (rafʿ). The firm mountains in the earth are fixed, and the stars in the sky are set firmly and adorn it. Growth in the earth is its splitting, as He said: ﴿That We poured water in abundance, then We split the earth in splitting﴾ [ʿAbasa: 25–26]. This is contrary to closing the rifts and eliminating them.

Once you know this, in the human being there are things placed (waḍʿ), things raised (rafʿ), and things fixed, like the nose and the ear; and things moving, like the eyeball and the tongue; and things whose openings are closed, like the roundness of the head and the wrapping membranes woven with a weak weave, like the peritoneum; and things that have openings and fissures, like the nostrils, the ear canal, the mouth, and others. So the One who is capable of these opposites in this cradle is in the seven strong heavens, not incapable of creating their likeness in these bodies.

**The first question:** The interrogative hamza (ʾa-) sometimes enters a statement without a waw in it, and sometimes enters it with a waw after it. Is there a difference between the two situations?

We say: there is a difference more subtle than what is apparent. It is that a speaker says: *ʾa-Zaydun fi al-dār baʿdu wa-qad ṭalaʿat al-shams?* (Is Zayd still in the house, and the sun has risen?), mentioning it as a denial. For the sky: building, adornment, and closing its rifts. Each one corresponds to one of the other. Spreading out corresponds to building, because spreading is placement (waḍʿ) and building is elevation (rafʿ). The second: regarding His saying ﴿a dead land﴾: we say that the feminine ending may be affixed to "dead" (mayt) and omitted when the feminine noun is described by it. This is because "mayt" is a lightened form of "mayyit", and "mayyit" is fa'il in the sense of fa'il/maf'ul... more precisely, the form fa'il in the sense of fa'il, so it is permissible to affix the feminine ending to it, because the form fa'il in the sense of maf'ul is treated equally, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed the mercy of God is near to the good-doers﴾ [al-A'raf: 56]. If it is asked: why did He treat the masculine and feminine alike in fa'il in the sense of maf'ul? We say: because the need to distinguish between the agent and the patient is stronger than the need to distinguish between a masculine patient and a feminine patient, both in view of meaning and in view of form. As for meaning, it is evident. As for form, the difference between the agent and the object is clear. Now, in fa'il, the agent is not distinguished by a letter, for fa'il comes in the sense of agent, like naṣīr and baṣīr, and in the sense of patient, like kasīr and asīr, and it is not distinguished by a letter upon difference except in the stronger case, so the weaker is not distinguished upon difference. The verification of this is that fa'il was set for a verbal meaning, while maf'ul was set for a real meaning. It is as if the speaker said: "They used the word maf'ul for that meaning, and they used the word fa'il in place of the word maf'ul," so fa'il became like one assigned to the patient, and maf'ul like one assigned to the meaning. Since change in the word follows change in meaning, maf'ul changed because it corresponds to the meaning, while fa'il did not change because at first it corresponds to the word. Whereas "balda" (town/inhabited land) originally involves life, since when land becomes living it becomes inhabited, and people settle in it and build it, so it becomes a town, and so He dropped the feminine ending, because the sense of agency is established in it, and what is in the sense of the agent does not take the feminine ending. This is a rare investigation.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus is the coming forth﴾, meaning: like the revival (al-khuruj, "the coming forth"). If it is said: it is the bringing forth (al-ikhraj) that is compared to revival, not the coming forth (al-khuruj), we say: its sense is: "We revived by it a dead land, and it split open and the plants came forth from it; thus it splits open and the dead come forth from it." Had they found improbable the raj' which is transitive (min al-muta'addi), it would have been fitting for Him to say: "Thus is the bringing forth (al-ikhraj)." And when He said ﴿Thus is the coming forth﴾, it was understood that they denied the return, so He said: ﴿Thus is the coming forth﴾.

We say: in this there is a subtle meaning according to the other view, namely that they found improbable the raj' which is transitive, in the sense of the bringing forth (al-ikhraj), while God affirmed the coming forth (al-khuruj). Both together convey emphasis, as a notice of the eloquence of the Qur'an, although they are self-evident and need no explanation. Its reasoning is that the raj' and the ikhraj are like the cause of the ruju' (return) and the khuruj (coming forth), and a cause, if it is negated, the effect is definitely negated; and if it exists, the effect may fail to follow it because of an impediment. You say: "I broke it, but it did not break," and it is figurative. And the effect, if it exists, its cause has existed; and if it is negated, the cause is not thereby negated, for the reason already stated. Once this is known, it is understood that they denied the existence of the cause and rejected it, and the effect is definitely negated upon the negation of the cause. So they went to the extreme and denied the matter entirely, because the negation of the cause is the negation of the effect. Thus God affirmed both matters through the khuruj, just as they negated both matters together through the negation of the ikhraj.

Then God Most High said: ﴿And We send down from the sky blessed water, and We produce thereby gardens and grain of harvest,﴾ ﴿and tall palm trees, with ranks of fruit-clusters﴾.

The "tall ones" (basiqat) are the lofty palm trees.

His saying: ﴿for it are spathes piled high﴾, meaning, its fruit-clusters are piled one upon another within their sheaths, like the ear of grain. And His saying ﴿so My warning came true﴾ means what God promised of the victory of the messengers over them and of their destruction.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Were We then wearied by the first creation? Rather they are in confusion about a new creation.﴾

The first: that it is an argument from the signs within the self (dalail al-anfus), because we have mentioned many times that the proofs are of the horizons (afaqiyyah) and of the self (nafsiyyah), as He said: ﴿We shall show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves﴾ [Fussilat: 53]. When God combined the proofs of the horizons, He joined some of them to others with the particle of conjunction waw, saying: ﴿And the earth—We spread it out﴾. Then in the proof from the self He mentioned the interrogative particle, and the fāʾ (fa, "then") after it indicates that those proofs are of one kind and this is of another kind, so He did not make this a follow-on to that. A similar pattern is observed at the end of Yasin, where He said: ﴿Has not man seen that We created him﴾ [Yasin: 77]. Then why did He not join the proof of the horizons here? We say, and God knows best: here they showed disbelief in the saying ﴿That is a far-off return﴾, so He argued by the greater thing, which is the creation of the heavens. Then He descended, as if He said: there is no need for that argument; rather within themselves there is proof of the possibility of that. In Surat Yasin He did not mention their disbelief, so He began with the nearer and ascended to the higher.

The second aspect: it is possible that by "the first creation" is meant the creation of the heavens, because it is the first creation. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky?﴾ and then said: ﴿Were We wearied﴾ by this creation. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 33]. This second aspect is supported by the fact that God, exalted is He, said after this verse: ﴿And We created man, and We know what his self whispers to him﴾. So it is like an argument from the creation of man, joined by the waw to what preceded of creation, which is the building of the sky, the spreading of the earth, the sending down of water, and the growing of gardens. The first: that both apply together, because the first one everyone knows and it is known in itself, whereas the new creation is not known in itself and not everyone knows it. Also, the speech is about them, and they were not knowledgeable of the new creation.

Furthermore, confusion (al-labs) is attributed to the matter, as we have said: it is said that this matter is evident and this matter is confused. Here He attributed the matter to them when He said ﴿they are in confusion﴾, because a thing may be behind a veil while the one looking at it has sight, so the matter becomes hidden from the viewpoint of the observer. Thus He said here: ﴿Rather they are in confusion﴾. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 50, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the agony of death will come in truth. That is what you were trying to avoid.﴾

That is, its intensity, which takes away the intellects and bewilders the minds. His saying "in truth" (bi-l-haqq) admits of several interpretations. The first: that what is meant by it is death, for it is true (haqq), as if the intensity of death brings death into presence; here the bāʾ (bi) is for transitivity (al-taʿdiyah), as one says: "So-and-so brought such-and-such" (jāʾa fulān bi-kadhā), meaning he caused it to be present. The second: that what is meant by "the truth" (al-haqq) is what was brought by way of religion, because it is true, and it becomes manifest at the intensity of death; there is no one who, in that state, does not display faith, but it is not accepted except from one who had it beforehand and believed in the unseen. The meaning of "bringing it" is that it makes it manifest, as one says: "the religion that the Prophet (ﷺ) brought," meaning he made it manifest. Since the intensity of death makes it manifest, it is said of it: "he brought it." The bāʾ in this case may be understood as meaning "accompanied by" (mulabbisah), as one says: "I came to you with a wide hope and a humble heart." His saying "That" (dhalika) may be a reference to death, and it may be a reference to the truth. "Hād ʿan al-ṭarīq" means he deviated from the path, that is, he turned away from it. The address has been said to be directed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is rejected; it has been said to be directed to the disbelievers, and this is closer; but the strongest view is that it is a general address to the listener, as if he were saying: "That is what you, O listener, were trying to avoid."

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the Horn will be blown; that is the Day of the Threat.﴾

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon His saying: ﴿And the agony of death will come﴾. Its meaning is either the first blast (al-nafkhah al-ūlā), so that it explains what will happen at the coming of the agony of death, or the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thāniyah), and this is more apparent, because His saying ﴿that is the Day of the Threat﴾ is more fitting with the second blast. In that case His saying ﴿And the agony of death will come﴾ refers to causing to die, and His saying ﴿And the Horn will be blown﴾ refers to the restoration and the bringing back to life.

As for His saying, the Exalted, (that), al-Zamakhsharī mentioned that it is a reference to the verbal noun (maṣdar) in His saying (And it will be blown), meaning: the time of that blowing is the Day of the Threat. This is weak, because if "yawm" were in the accusative case, what we have mentioned would be apparent; but with "yawm" in the nominative case, it conveys that "that" is the very day itself, and a verbal noun cannot be the very time, rather it occurs within time. So the better view is to say: "that" refers to the time understood from His saying:

(And it will be blown), because the verb, just as it indicates the verbal noun, also indicates time. It is as if He, the Exalted, had said: "That time is the Day of the Threat." And the Threat is what He promised with regard to the gathering, the giving (of accounts), and the requital.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness﴾. We have already explained earlier that the driver (sā'iq) is the one who drives it to the place of standing (al-mawqif) and from there to its seat, and the witness (shahīd) is the recording angel (al-kātib). The driver accompanies both the righteous (al-barr) and the wicked (al-fājir): as for the righteous, he is driven to Paradise, and as for the wicked, he is driven to the Fire. And God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups﴾ [al-Zumar: 71], and ﴿And those who feared their Lord will be driven to Paradise in groups﴾ [al-Zumar: 73].

And His saying, ﴿You were certainly heedless of this﴾, may be on the assumption of a speaker, meaning: it is said to him, or it is said to him, ﴿You were certainly...﴾, as in His saying, ﴿And its keepers will say to them﴾ (Az-Zumar 39:73), and His saying, ﴿It will be said: Enter the gates of Hell﴾ (Az-Zumar 39:72). The address is general. As for the disbeliever, he is known to be included in this ruling. As for the believer, he increases in knowledge, what was hidden from him becomes manifest to him, and he sees his knowledge as certainty, the sight of one who takes lesson with certainty. Thus, in relation to those circumstances and the severity of the terrors, he is like one who is heedless. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 50, verse 25:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿forbidding of good﴾.

In it there are two opinions:

The first: he is one who greatly withholds wealth that is obligatory, and even if it is from disbelief, he is the most denying of the proofs of Allah's oneness despite their strength and clarity. So he was severely disbelieving and obstinate (ʿanid), since he denied the manifest matter and the clear truth, and he was greatly ungrateful (kufran), because ingratitude was present in him at every blessing (ʿanid) which he denies despite its abundance, withholding it from the one entitled to it who asks for it. The "good" here is wealth, so it is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakah﴾ [Fussilat: 6], where He began with explaining polytheism and followed it with refraining from giving zakah. On this view there is a strong connection if we take "kafir" to mean ingrate, as if he is saying: he ungratefully rejected the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, and did not pay any of them as thanks for His blessings.

The second: he is one who strongly prevents [people] from faith, so he is ﴿forbidding of good﴾, and that is faith, which is pure good, from entering the hearts of the servants. On this view there is a strong connection if we take "kafir" to mean disbelief, as if he is saying: he disbelieved in Allah, and was not content with his disbelief until he prevented good from others.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿transgressor﴾.

In it there are two opinions:

The first: that his saying ﴿transgressor﴾ is connected to ﴿forbidding of good﴾ in the sense of withholding zakah. Its meaning is that he did not pay what was obligatory and exceeded that to take the forbidden as well, through usury and theft, as was the custom of the polytheists.

The second: that his saying ﴿transgressor﴾ is connected to ﴿forbidding of good﴾ in the sense of preventing faith, as if he is saying: he prevented faith and was not content with it until he exceeded its bounds, humiliated the one who believed and harmed him, and aided the one who disbelieved and sheltered him.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿doubtful﴾.

In it there are two opinions:

The first: one who has doubt, and this is on our view that the disbeliever is greatly ungrateful and the one who forbids is the withholder of zakah. As if he is saying: he does not give zakah because he is in doubt about the Hereafter and the reward, so he says: I will not bring wealth closer without return.

The second: ﴿doubtful﴾ means one who places others into doubt by casting suspicion, and the verb "arabah" came with both meanings together. In the verse there is another arrangement different from what we mentioned, namely that it may be said: this is an explanation of the states of disbelief in relation to Allah, to the Messenger of Allah, and to the Last Day. So His saying: ﴿disbelieving, obstinate﴾ is an indication of his state with Allah: he disbelieves in Him and opposes His signs. His saying: ﴿forbidding of good, transgressor﴾ is an indication of his state with the Messenger of Allah: he prevents people from following him and from spending on those who are with him, and he exceeds bounds by harm and abundant ridicule. His saying: (doubtful) is an indication of his state in relation to the Last Day: he is in doubt about it and suspects, and does not think that the Hour is established. Now, if it is said that His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Cast into Hell every obstinate disbeliever﴾ ﴿forbidding of good﴾ and so on requires that the casting be specific to the one in whom all these attributes are gathered together, while disbelief alone is sufficient to bring about casting into Hell and the command to it, we say: His saying, the Exalted, ﴿every disbeliever, obstinate﴾ does not mean a distinguishing description, as one says: give to the scholar, the ascetic; rather it means a descriptive attribute that shows the described being characterized by it, either by way of praise or by way of blame, as one says: this is Hatim the generous. So His saying ﴿every disbeliever, obstinate﴾ indicates that the disbeliever is obstinate and forbidding of good; the disbeliever is a disbeliever because the signs of oneness are manifest and Allah's blessings upon His servant are abundant; and he is obstinate and forbidding of good because he praises his own religion and disparages the religion of truth, so he prevents; and doubtful because he is skeptical about the gathering. Thus every disbeliever is described by these attributes.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 50, verses 26–27:

Allah's words: ﴿Who set up with Allah another god, so cast him into the severe punishment.﴾

In this there are three possibilities (awjuh):

The first: it is a substitution (badal) for His words: ﴿every obstinate disbeliever﴾.

The second: it is a conjunction (atf) upon: ﴿every obstinate disbeliever﴾.

The third: it is a conjunction upon His words: ﴿Cast into Hell﴾, as if He said: "Cast into Hell every obstinate disbeliever," meaning: "And the one who set up with Allah another god, so cast him, after you have cast him into Hell, into severe punishment from the punishment of Hell."

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿His companion said: "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress; but he was in far error."﴾

This is a response to an unstated statement. It is as if the disbeliever, when he is cast into the Fire, says: "Our Lord, my Satan made me transgress," and then the Satan says: "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress." This is indicated by Allah's words after this: ﴿He said: "Do not dispute before Me"﴾ [Qaf: 28]. Disputing requires speech from both sides. And in this case, as Allah said in this surah and in Sad: ﴿They will say: "Rather, you! No welcome for you"﴾ [Sad: 60], and His words: ﴿They will say: "Our Lord, whoever set this forth for us, increase him in doubled punishment in the Fire"﴾ [Sad: 61], up to His words: ﴿Indeed, that is true—the disputing of the people of the Fire﴾ [Sad: 64].

Concerning this there are several issues (masa'il):

The first issue: Al-Zamakhshari said: the intended meaning of "companion" (qarin) in the preceding verse is the Satan, not the angel who is a witness and an attendant (qa'id), and he argued for this with this verse. Others said the intended meaning is the angel, not the Satan. This can serve as evidence for the one who says so. Its explanation is that: in the first place, if the intended meaning were the Satan, then His words ﴿This is what is with me, ready﴾ would mean: "This person is with me, ready, prepared for the Fire, which I have prepared by my seduction." Al-Zamakhshari explicitly stated this in his interpretation of that verse. On this basis, His words ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him transgress﴾ [Qaf: 27] would contradict His words "I prepared him."

Al-Zamakhshari may answer: the response to this is from two aspects:

The first: that one can say the Satan says "I prepared him" in the sense of "I adorned the matter for him," and "I did not compel him"; so both statements are valid from the Satan.

The second: that the reference is to two states. In the first state, "I only did that to him to display vengeance against the children of Adam, and to confirm what I said: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾." Then when he sees the punishment, and that he is a partner in it with him, and that he has a punishment for the seduction, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So the truth is, and the truth I say: "I will surely fill Hell with you and with whoever follows you"﴾ [Sad: 84–85], he then says ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him transgress﴾, and so he retracts his statement at the appearance of the punishment.

The second issue: Here He said ﴿His companion said﴾ without a waw, whereas in the first verse He said ﴿And his companion said﴾ with the conjunctive waw. That is because in the first case the reference was to two combined meanings, namely that every soul at that time comes with a driver (sa'iq), and the witness (shahid) says that statement; whereas in the second case there are no two combined meanings present there such that it would be introduced with waw. The fa' in His words ﴿so cast him into the punishment﴾ does not suit His words ﴿His companion said: "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress"﴾ in a way that would require conjunction with waw.

The third issue: The speaker here is one, and He said "Our Lord" (rabbana) and not "My Lord" (Rabbi). In many places, though the speaker is one, He said "Rabbi," as in His words: ﴿He said: "My Lord, show me that I may look upon You"﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], and Noah's words: ﴿My Lord, forgive me﴾ [Sad: 35], and His words: ﴿She said: "My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise"﴾ [al-Tahrim: 11], and beyond that, and His words: ﴿He said: "My Lord, then give me respite until the day they are resurrected"﴾ [Sad: 79]. We say that in all those places the speaker is a petitioner (talib), and it is not fitting for a petitioner to say: "O my Lord, prolong my life, single me out, and give me such-and-such." Rather he says, "Give us," because His being Lord does not suit singling out the petitioner. As for this place, it is a place of awe and majesty and presenting one's condition, not of request; so he said: ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him transgress﴾.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿But he was in far error.﴾

That is, that was not by his misleading him; rather he was astray, deeply immersed in error, and so he transgressed. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: What is the reason for describing error as "far" (ba'id)? We say: the one who is astray may be more astray from the road; when he persists in error and remains in it for a period, he becomes far from the goal greatly. And when one knows he is in error, he falls short on the road from nearby, so he is not far from the goal by much. Thus His words ﴿in far error﴾ are the description of the verbal noun (masdar) with what is used to describe the agent, as one says "a truthful speech" and "a pleased life," meaning: an error that has distance. When an error's range is extended and the one astray is lost in it for a long time, it becomes evident and the error becomes clear; for whoever swerves from the road and goes far from it, the signs and directions become confused for him, he does not see the very goal, and it becomes clear to him that he has strayed from the road, and perhaps he falls into valleys and deserts, and the signs of error appear to him—unlike one who has swerved only a little. Allah, exalted is He, has described error with both descriptions in many places: He said once "in clear error" (dalal mubin), and another time He said ﴿in far error﴾.

The second issue: His words, exalted is He, ﴿But he was in far error﴾ refer to His words ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [al-Hijr: 40], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, My servants—you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Hijr: 42]; that is, they were not among the servants, so He made them the people of obstinacy. And had they had a foothold of truthfulness on Your path, I would have had no power over them. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: How did he say "I did not make him transgress" when he had said ﴿I will surely mislead them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 39]? We say: the answer to this is from three aspects: two have already been mentioned in the defense of what al-Zamakhshari said, and the third is that the intended meaning of His words ﴿I will mislead them﴾ is: "I will keep them perpetually in misguidance," just as when a person who is astray is told by someone, "You are on the right path, so do not abandon it," it is said that he misleads him in this way. Here too, and His words ﴿I did not make him transgress﴾ mean: the beginning of the misguidance was not from me.
