When an error's range is extended and the one astray is lost in it for a long time, it becomes evident and the error becomes clear; for whoever swerves from the road and goes far from it, the signs and directions become confused for him, he does not see the very goal, and it becomes clear to him that he has strayed from the road, and perhaps he falls into valleys and deserts, and the signs of error appear to him—unlike one who has swerved only a little. Allah, exalted is He, has described error with both descriptions in many places: He said once "in clear error" (dalal mubin), and another time He said ﴿in far error﴾.

The second issue: His words, exalted is He, ﴿But he was in far error﴾ refer to His words ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [al-Hijr: 40], and His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, My servants—you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Hijr: 42]; that is, they were not among the servants, so He made them the people of obstinacy. And had they had a foothold of truthfulness on Your path, I would have had no power over them. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: How did he say "I did not make him transgress" when he had said ﴿I will surely mislead them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 39]? We say: the answer to this is from three aspects: two have already been mentioned in the defense of what al-Zamakhshari said, and the third is that the intended meaning of His words ﴿I will mislead them﴾ is: "I will keep them perpetually in misguidance," just as when a person who is astray is told by someone, "You are on the right path, so do not abandon it," it is said that he misleads him in this way. Here too, and His words ﴿I did not make him transgress﴾ mean: the beginning of the misguidance was not from me.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said, "Do not dispute in My presence."﴾

We have already mentioned that this indicates there was speech before His saying: ﴿His companion said, "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress"﴾, which is the saying of the one cast into the Fire: "Our Lord, he made me transgress." And His saying ﴿Do not dispute in My presence﴾ implies, by its meaning, that the disputing should have taken place before standing in His presence.

And His exalted saying: ﴿And I had already sent forward to you the warning﴾.

This is a confirmation of the prohibition of disputing and a clarification that it is of no benefit, as if He is saying: "I had already told you that if you follow Satan you will enter the Fire, and you did follow him."

If it is asked, what is the grammatical status of the particle bāʾ (with) in His saying ﴿with the warning﴾? We say there are several views:

First: it is superfluous (zāʾidah), as in His saying ﴿grows with the oil﴾ according to the view of one who says it is superfluous there, and His saying ﴿and sufficient is Allah﴾ [an-Nisa: 6].

Second: it is transitive (muʿaddiyah), so that qaddamtu means taqaddamtu (I went forward), as in His saying ﴿O you who have believed, do not put forward [anything] before Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hujurat: 1].

Third: there is an implied element in the speech, its estimate being: "And I had already sent forward to you, accompanied by the warning," so that the thing sent forward is His saying ﴿the word is not changed in My presence﴾, meaning the thing sent forward is His saying: "The word is not changed in My presence."

Fourth: it denotes accompaniment, as the speaker says: "I bought the horse with its bridle and saddle," meaning together with it. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "I sent forward to you what is obligatory together with the warning against abandoning it, through admonition."

His exalted saying ﴿The word is not changed in My presence﴾ admits of two possibilities:

One: that the phrase "in My presence" (ladayya) is connected to "the word" (al-qawl), meaning: ﴿the word is not changed in My presence﴾.

Two: that it is connected to His saying "is not changed" (yubaddalu), meaning that no change occurs in My presence. On the first possibility, regarding the word that is in His presence, there are several views:

First: when they said "until what was said concerning them is changed," [they said] "Cast them" by the word of Allah after their excuse, "Do not cast it," so He, exalted is He, said: this word is not changed in My presence. Likewise His saying: ﴿It will be said: Enter the gates of Hell﴾ [az-Zumar: 72], for there is no alteration of it.

Second: it is His saying ﴿But the word from Me has come into effect: I will surely fill Hell﴾ [as-Sajdah: 13], meaning there is no alteration of this word.

Third: there is no breaking of Allah's threat, just as there is no breaking of Allah's promise. This refutes the Murji'ah, who said that what came in the Qur'an of threat is merely intimidation, and Allah does not actualize any of it. They said: the Generous, when He promises, fulfills and completes, and when He threatens, He breaks it and pardons.

Fourth: the prior decree is not changed, that this one is wretched and this one is happy, from the time I created the servants: I said, "This one is wretched and will work the works of the wretched, and this one is pious and will work the works of the pious," and that word, with Me, has no alteration by the striving of any striver, and there is no happiness except by the success of Allah, exalted is He.

As for the second possibility, then in "is not changed" there are also several views:

First: it is not lied about in My presence, nor is it fabricated before Me, for I am All-Knowing: I know who transgressed and who caused transgression, who was a transgressor and who was the greater transgressor. So your saying "my devil made me transgress" will not benefit you, nor will the devil's saying: ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him transgress﴾.

Second: it is an indication of the meaning of His exalted saying: ﴿Return behind you and seek light﴾ [al-Hadid: 13], as if He, exalted is He, said: "If you had wished that I not speak and cast you into the severe punishment, you would have changed this earlier by changing disbelief into belief before you stood before Me. But now, the word is not changed in My presence, as we said regarding His saying ﴿He said, 'Do not dispute in My presence'﴾: the meaning is that your disputing should have occurred before this, when I said: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy﴾ [Fatir: 6]."

Third: its meaning is that disbelief is not changed into belief in My presence, for belief at the time of despair is not accepted. So your saying "Our Lord and our God" will not benefit you. Whoever has uttered the word of disbelief, his saying "Our Lord, we did not associate" does not benefit him, nor his saying "Our Lord, we believed." His exalted saying ﴿the word is not changed﴾ is an indication of the negation of the present state, as if He, exalted is He, says: "The word is not changed before Me today," because "mā" (not) when it enters upon the present-tense verb negates the present. The speaker says: "What are you doing tomorrow?" One answers: "mā afʿalu shayʾan" (I do nothing), meaning in the present. And if the speaker says: "What will he do tomorrow?" It is said: "lā yafʿalu shayʾan" or "lan yafʿala shayʾan," when more explicit clarification of the negation is intended.

If it is asked: is there a semantic explanation showing the difference between "mā" and "lā" in meaning? We say: yes. The word "lā" is more indicative of negation, because it is established for negation, and what is similar to it, like the prohibition, does not, except by way of deletion or implication, indicate affirmation; in sum, it is by way of metaphor, as in His saying "lā uqsimu" [al-Balad: 1]. As for "mā," it is not purely for negation, because it occurs for other meanings when it is a noun. Negation in the present does not entail absolute negation, since with present negation there may be affirmation in the future, as one says: "He does not do anything now, but he will do it, God willing." Therefore "mā" was specified for what is not purely negation, since it is not purely for negation. One cannot say that "lā" is for negation in the future and affirmation in the present, so that "mā" alone is used for the future negation which is not purely negation; because we say: that is not so, for it is not permissible to say "Zayd does not do, and does [it] now." Yes, it is permissible to say "He does not do it tomorrow, but does it now," because your saying "tomorrow" makes the time specified, so your saying "does not do" was not negation in the future generally, but in some part of the future. In our example we said "mā yafʿalu wa-sayafʿalu," and we did not say "sayafʿalu ghadan wa-baʿda ghad," but rather here we negated in the present and affirmed in the future without distinguishing a particular future time from another. Its converse example is that one says "Zayd does not do," while he does it, without specification or distinction; and it is known that this is not permissible.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 50, verse 29:

And His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And I am not ever unjust to the servants﴾, is appropriate to what preceded on both interpretations. As for if we say that what is meant by His saying "with Me" (ladayya) is that His saying "Cast him" and the saying of the one who says, in His saying, ﴿It will be said: Enter the gates of Hell﴾ [az-Zumar: 72], are not to be changed, then it is clear, because God, the Exalted, has explained that His saying, ﴿Cast into Hell﴾, applies only to the stubborn disbelievers, so He Himself is not unjust to the servants. And as for if we say that what is meant is that ﴿the word is not changed with Me﴾, but rather the changing was required before standing before Me, then likewise, because He warned beforehand, and did not punish except after sending messengers and making the ways clear. And in this there are linguistic (lafziyya) and semantic (ma'nawiyya) discussions.

As for the linguistic ones, they concern the bāʾ (ba) in His saying "laysa bi-ẓallāmin" (is not unjust), and the lām in His saying "lil-ʿabīd" (to the servants). As for the bāʾ, we say: the bāʾ enters the direct object where the attachment of the verb to it is not evident, and its entry is not permitted where it is in the utmost clarity; and both entry and omission are permitted where it is neither in utmost clarity nor in utmost obscurity. So one does not say "ḍarabtu bi-Zaydin" (I struck Zayd), because the attachment of the verb to Zayd is clear; and one does not say "kharajtu wa dhahabtu Zaydan" in place of "kharajtu wa dhahabtu bi-Zaydin," because the attachment of the verb to Zayd in both is hidden. And one says "shakartuhu lahu" (I thanked him for it) for the intermediacy. Likewise, the predicate of "mā," since it is made similar to the object, and there is no utmost clarity in its being a verb, because the attachment of the pronouns that attach to past verbs, such as the tā' and nūn in your saying "lasta, lastum, lastunna, lasnā," makes it correct that it is a verb, as in your saying "kuntu, kunnā"; but in the future the difference becomes clear, where we say "yakūnu, takūnu, and kun," and we do not say that with "laysa" and what resembles it. So they became like a verb whose attachment to the object is not evident in the utmost clarity, and so it is permitted to say "laysa Zaydun jāhilan" and "laysa Zaydun bi-jāhilin," just as one says "masaḥtuhu" and "masaḥtu bihi," and other things that are transitive by themselves and by the bāʾ. But it is not permitted to say "kāna Zaydun bi-kharijin" or "ṣāra ʿAmrun bi-dārijin," because "ṣāra" and "kāna" are verbs whose clarity is in the utmost clarity, unlike "laysa" and the negating "mā." And this supports the view of the one who said "mā hādhā basharan" (this is not a human), and this is clear.

The second discussion: If someone says: it should not be permitted to omit the bāʾ from the predicate of "mā," just as it is not permitted to add the bāʾ to the predicate of "kāna," while the predicate of "laysa" permits both. The statement of this objection is that "kāna," since it is a verb in clear form, we made it like "ḍaraba," so we prohibited the entry of the bāʾ into its predicate just as we prohibited it into its object. And it is not, because it is a verb in one respect, looking at our saying "lasta, lasnā, lastum," and it is not a clear verb looking at the forms of the future and the imperative, that we made it intermediate and permitted the entry of the bāʾ into its predicate and its omission, as we said regarding the object of "shakartuhu" and "shakartu lahu." And "mā," since it is not a verb in any respect, should be like the verb that is not transitive to the object except by a particle, and its predicate should not come except with the bāʾ, just as the object of "dhahaba" does not come except with the bāʾ. And this is supported by the fact that we distinguished between "mā," "laysa," and "kāna," and gave each one a rank that the others do not have. So we permitted the postponement of "kāna" in wording, where we permitted one to say "Zaydun kharijan kāna," but we did not permit "Zaydun kharijan laysa," because "kāna" is a clear verb and "laysa" is not less than it in clarity. And we did not permit the postponement of "mā" from either half of the sentence either, unlike "laysa," where one may not say "Zaydun mā bi-ẓallāmin," unless he repeats what it refers back to, saying "Zaydun mā huwa bi-ẓallāmin." Thus between them there is an arrangement that is to be noted, and it is not postponed from either half, nor is it postponed in the sentence entirely; and "kāna" would be postponed entirely because of what we mentioned of clarity and obscurity. Thus the same applies to the addition of the bāʾ: it should not be valid to omit the predicate of "mā" from the bāʾ; with "laysa" both are permitted; with "kāna" addition is not permitted. And this is the reliable view in the dialect of the Banū Tamīm, where they said: what follows "mā," when made a predicate, requires the bāʾ to be attached to it; if the bāʾ does not enter it, then that is inflected as a subject (mubtada') or in another way, and is not a predicate. The answer to the objection is that we say: most often the bāʾ enters the predicate of "mā," especially in the Qur'an. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you are not one to guide the blind out of their error﴾ [an-Naml: 81]; ﴿And you are not one to make the deaf hear﴾ [Fatir: 22]; ﴿And they are not ones to come out﴾ [al-Baqarah: 167]; ﴿And I am not ever unjust﴾ [Qaf: 29]. As for the obligation, no, because what resembles "laysa" agrees with it in meaning in reality and differs from it in accidents, which is the attaching of the tā' and nūn; and as for meaning, both of them negate the present. So resemblance requires permissibility of omission, and difference requires obligation of addition; but that requirement is stronger, because it returns to the real matter, and this returns to the accidental matter, and what is in the essence is stronger than what is by accident. As for the postponement and anteposition, it does not necessitate the obligation of adding the bāʾ. As for the discussion of the lām, we say: the lām is to realize the meaning of the idāfa (annexation). One says "ghulāmu Zaydin" (Zayd's servant) and "ghulāmun li-Zaydin" (a servant of Zayd), and this is in genuine annexations with the tanwīn affirmed in it. As for the verbal annexations, such as our saying "ḍāribu Zaydin" (one who strikes Zayd) and "qātilu ʿAmrin" (killer of ʿAmr), the annexation in it is not semantic (ma'nawiyya). So when the one who strikes is removed from being annexed by affirming the tanwīn, it would have been required to return to the original, and what was annexed to by the agent would be put in the accusative as the object, and the lām would not be brought, because then the annexation would no longer remain in form, and it would not be an annexation in meaning. However, the active participle is lower in rank than the verb, so its attachment to the object is weaker than the attachment of the verb to the object, and it became of the class of weakly attached verbs, since we showed the permissibility of transferring it to the object with a particle and without a particle. Therefore it is permitted to say "ḍāribun Zaydan" or "ḍāribun li-Zaydin," just as "masaḥtuhu" and "masaḥtu bihi," and "shakartuhu" and "shakartu lahu" are permitted; and that is when the object precedes, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If you are interpreters of dreams, interpret﴾ [Yusuf: 43], due to weakness. As for the semantic discussions, they are several:

The first: "ẓallām" is an intensive form of "ẓālim" (wrongdoer), and affirming it entails affirming the root of injustice; if someone says "huwa kadhdhāb" (he is a great liar), it entails that he is a liar who lies much. But negating it does not entail negating the root of lying, since one may say "so-and-so is not a great liar, a frequent liar, but he lies occasionally." So in His saying, ﴿And I am not ever unjust﴾, it is not understood from it that the root of injustice is negated, and God is not unjust; so what is the explanation? We say: the answer to it is from three aspects.

The first: that "ẓallām" means "ẓālim," like "tammār" means "tāmir" (dealer in dates), and then the lām in His saying "lil-ʿabīd" is to realize the relation, because the fa'āl then means "one possessing injustice." This is a good aspect, derived from the Imam Zayn al-Din, may God prolong his benefits.

The second: what az-Zamakhshari mentioned, which is that this is a hypothetical matter, as if God, the Exalted, says: If I were to wrong My weak servant, who is the locus of mercy, that would be the utmost injustice, and I am not like that. So negating His being an ẓallām entails negating His being a ẓālim. And this aspect is confirmed by the mention of the word "servants," where He says: ﴿And I am not ever unjust to the servants﴾, meaning on that Day when Hell is filled despite its vastness, until it cries out and says: there is no strength left in me for them, and there is no place left in me for them, ﴿Is there any more?﴾ — a question of amazement. So on that Day, although I cast into it an uncountable number, I am not, because of the abundance of punishment, one who is greatly unjust. This is appropriate. That is because He restricted the negation by time, where He said: "I am not ever unjust on the Day when We say," meaning: and I am not unjust at all times as well; and He restricted it to the servants, where He said: ﴿And I am not ever unjust to the servants﴾ and did not make it absolute. Likewise He restricted the negation to a kind of injustice and did not make it absolute. So it does not entail that He is a wrongdoer at another time, or toward other than the servants, even if He restricted it. The benefit of the restriction is that it is closer to affirmation than generalization.

The third: this shows that restriction by mention does not indicate negation of what is other than it, because He negated being an ẓallām and it did not entail negating being a ẓālim; and He negated being an ẓallām to the servants, and it did not entail negating being an ẓallām to others, just as He said regarding the human: ﴿So among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ [Fatir: 32].

The second discussion: He said here, ﴿And I am not ever unjust to the servants﴾ without an annexation, and He said, ﴿And you are not one to guide the blind﴾ [an-Naml: 81], ﴿And you are not one to make hear those in the graves﴾ [Fatir: 22], with an annexation. So what is the difference between them? We say: speech may come first in the form of generality, then be restricted for some matter, not for the purpose of restriction. A speaker says: so-and-so gives and withholds, and his purpose is generalization; if a questioner asks, "Whom does he give to, and whom does he withhold from?", he says, "Zayd and ʿAmr," and brings the restrictor not for the purpose of restriction. And it may come first in the form of particularity, so he says: so-and-so gives Zayd his wealth. Having known this, His saying, ﴿And I am not ever unjust﴾, is a statement which, if it were confined to it, would be general; so He brought the word "servants," not because the absence of injustice is specific to them, but because they are closer to being the locus of injustice than God Himself. As for the Prophet ﷺ, he was in himself a guide, and he only meant to negate that particular thing, so He said: ﴿And you are not one to guide the blind﴾ [an-Naml: 81], and did not say "you are not a guide"; and likewise His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is not God sufficient for His servant?﴾ [az-Zumar: 36].

The third discussion: "the servants" may be understood to mean the disbelievers, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Alas for the servants! No messenger comes to them﴾ [Ya-Sin: 30], meaning: I punish them; and I am not unjust to them. And it may be understood to mean the believers. Its aspect is that God, the Exalted, says: If I were to change the word and show mercy to the disbeliever, I would be unjust in imposing obligations on My servants, the believers, because I restrained them from desires for the sake of this Day. If whoever did not do what the believer did receives what the believer receives, then his doing what he did of faith and worship would be of no benefit. This is the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The companions of the Fire and the companions of the Garden are not equal; the companions of the Garden are the triumphant﴾ [al-Hashr: 20], and the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ [az-Zumar: 9], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Not equal are the sitters among the believers, other than those with a harm﴾ [an-Nisa': 95]. And it may be understood to mean generality.

Then God, the Exalted, said:

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the Day We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Are there any more?"﴾.

What is the governing element (al-'amil) of "yawma" (on the day)? There are several views.

The first: "I am not at all a wrongdoer" (ma ana bi-zallam mutlaqan).

The second: the time, since He said "I am not a wrongdoer on such a day" and did not say "I am not a wrongdoer at all times," and its explanation has already passed. If it is asked, "What is the benefit of the specification?", we say: a specific negation is closer to being believed than a general negation, because what is being imagined is that. For the shallow-sighted person says: "On the day God makes His weak servant enter Hell, He is a wrongdoer toward him," and does not say: "On the day He created him, provided him with sustenance and nurtured him, He is a wrongdoer." He imagines that He wrongs His servant by putting him into the Fire, but does not imagine that He wrongs Himself or others than the servants mentioned, and he imagines that He is one who puts a great multitude into the Fire, which no limit contains and no count reaches, and leaves them in it for a time without end, being greatly unjust. So He negated what is imagined rather than what is not imagined. His words ﴿Are you filled?﴾ are an explanation confirming His words ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾ [as-Sajdah: 13]. As for His words ﴿Are there any more?﴾, there are two views:

One of them: it is to show how much Hell has taken in of those who entered, just as one who beats another severely, or insults him with a vile and gross insult, and the one beaten says: "Is there anything else left?" This is indicated by His words "I will surely fill," because filling must occur, so no empty place remains in Hell until it seeks more.

The second: it is that Hell seeks increase. In that case, if someone asks, "How is the meaning of His words 'I will surely fill' understood alongside this?", we say: the answer to this comes in several ways:

One of them: this statement may occur before all have entered. There is a subtle point in this: Hell rages against the disbelievers and seeks them, then a place remains for the disobedient believers. Hell seeks to be filled because it thinks that one of the disbelievers remains outside, so the disobedient believer is made to enter, his faith cools its heat, and his certainty calms its rage, so it becomes still. On this is interpreted what is reported in some traditions, that Hell seeks increase until the Almighty places His foot in it, and the believer is "jabbar" (one who compels), proud over all other than God, yet humbly submissive to God.

The second: that Hell first seeks breadth in itself, then more of those who enter, because it thinks that one of the disbelievers remains.

The third: that fullness has degrees. When a measure is filled without pressing, it is correct to say "it was filled" and "it became full"; but when it is pressed down, it can hold more without this being inconsistent with its having been full at first. Likewise in Hell: God fills it, then it seeks an increase, narrowing the place upon them and increasing the punishment. "Al-mazid" may be used in the sense of the passive participle, i.e., "Is there anyone left by whom it may be increased?"

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing, not far away.﴾ It means "nearby" (qarīban), or it means "near" (qarīb) in the sense of a [different] grammatical form, and the first is more apparent. On this verse there are several issues.

The first issue: what is the sense of "bringing near," given that Paradise is a place, and places are approached while they themselves do not approach? We say: the answer to this has several aspects.

The first: Paradise is not moved or transported, and the believer is not commanded on that day to travel to it despite its distance; rather, God folds up the distance between the believer and Paradise, and this is the "bringing near." If it is said: then according to this, the bringing near of Paradise to the believer is no more fitting than the bringing near of the believer to Paradise, so what is the benefit in His saying "Paradise was brought near"? We say: it is an honouring of the believer, as if He, exalted is He, intended to show the nobility of the God-fearing believer, that he is one to whom [Paradise] is brought and near whom it is drawn.

The second: it was brought near to attainability in entry, not in the sense of spatial nearness. It is said that someone seeks a weighty matter from a king, and the king is far from that; then when he sees signs of the fulfilment of his need, it is said "the king has been brought near," and "I have not ceased to report your condition to him until you brought him near." Likewise, Paradise was far from attainability, because in what it contains it has no price, and the accountable person has no power to attain it except by the grace of God, exalted is He, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "None of you will enter Paradise except by the grace of God." It was said: "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even I."

According to this, His saying "ghayra" (not) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl); its implied sense is "it was brought near to attainability," and it was not far in distance so that it could be asked how it was brought near.

The third: God, exalted is He, is able to move Paradise from the heaven to the earth, so He brings it near to the believer. As for if we say that it was brought near, its meaning is that its excellences were gathered together, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Therein is whatever your souls desire﴾ [Fussilat: 31].

The second issue: according to this aspect, and according to our saying "brought near" in the sense of attainability and entry, it admits two aspects:

One of them: that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿was brought near﴾ refers to that day, and it had not been [brought near] before that. As for the gathering of excellences, God may increase in it the adornment of the time of entry; and as for attainability, entry before that was deemed remote, if God had not decreed the entry of the believers into Paradise in this world and promised it in the Hereafter, so it was brought near on that day.

The other: that the meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and Paradise was brought near﴾ is that it was brought near in this world, either in the sense of gathering excellences, because it is created and everything has been created in it, or in the sense of bringing attainability near, because it is attained by a good word; or if the bringing near is taken as spatial nearness, then it is to be understood only as referring to that time, i.e., it was brought near on that day to the God-fearing.

The second issue: if it is taken as spatial nearness, what is the benefit of restricting it to the God-fearing, given that the believer and the unbeliever are in one place of assembly? We say: it may be that two persons are in one place, and there is another place which is very near to one of them and very far from the other. An example: a man with cut legs and a healthy man of great speed, if they are gathered in one place and before them is something that the hand cannot reach by stretching, then that is far from the one with cut legs and very near to the one who runs. Or we say: if two persons are gathered in one place, and one of them is enclosed by an iron barrier, and something is placed near him which his hand cannot reach by stretching, while the other is not enclosed by that barrier, it is correct to say: it is far from the one who is barred and near to the one who is favoured and fortunate. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿not far away﴾ may be in the accusative as an adverb of place: one says "sit not far from me," i.e., a place not far. According to this, His saying "not far away" gives emphasis, because the near may be far in relation to something; a place that is a day's journey away is near in relation to distant lands and far in relation to the parks of the city. So if someone asks: which is nearer, the Farthest Mosque or the city that is at the farthest west or east? It is said to him: the Farthest Mosque is near. And if he asks: which of them is nearer to you, it or the city? It is said to him: it is far. So His saying, exalted is He: "And Paradise was brought near… not far away" means: it was brought near with real nearness, not relative nearness, such that it is not said of it that it is far from him, by comparison or by correspondence. It may also be in the accusative as a circumstantial state, its implied sense being: it drew near, the condition being that this is the utmost nearness; or we say, on this aspect, the meaning of "was brought near" is "drew near," while it is "not far away," so both meanings are obtained together: the nearness and the drawing near. Or the intended meaning is nearness and attainability, not of place, so two meanings are obtained: spatial nearness by His saying "not far away," and attainability by His saying "was brought near." As for His saying "not far away" together with His saying "was brought near" in the feminine, it admits several aspects:

The first: if we say that "ghayr" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, its implied sense being "a place not far."

The second: the masculine here is as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed the mercy of God is near﴾ [al-A'raf: 56], treating fa'īl in the sense of fā'il in the manner of fa'īl in the sense of maf'ūl.

The third: that "ghayr" is said to be in the accusative as a verbal noun, being an attribute of an implied verbal noun, its implied sense being: "Paradise was brought near with a bringing near not far," i.e., not far from our power, for we have mentioned that Paradise is a place, and a place is not brought near but is approached; so He said: the bringing near is not far from our power, for We fold up the distance between the two.

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿This is what you were promised﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a parenthetical clause (jumla mu'tarida) placed between two statements. It is also possible to say that it is an independent statement (kalam mustaqill), and its basis is that it is taken in terms of meaning, not of what is promised: one says to the one who is promised, "This is yours," and it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "This is what I said it would be for you."

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿for every oft-returning, watchful one﴾, as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "you were promised." Likewise, if it is read with the letter ya', its implied sense is: "This is for every oft-returning one," as a substitute for the pronoun. The awwab (oft-returning) is the one who returns much; it has been said he is the one who returns from sins and seeks forgiveness. The hafiz (watchful) is the one who guards his repentance from being broken. It is also possible to say that the awwab is the one who returns to God in his thought, and the hafiz is the one who guards God in his remembrance, meaning: he returns to Him through reflection, so he sees every thing as coming to be through Him and originating from Him; then, when he reaches Him, he guards Him so that he does not forget Him in times of ease and blessing. Both awwab and hafiz are in the form of intensives (min bab al-mubalagha), meaning one who returns very often and guards very strictly. There are other, subtler aspects: that the awwab is the one who turns back from following his desires toward preoccupation with other than God, and the hafiz is the one who, when he attains Him with the noblest of his faculties, does not abandon Him, thereby perfecting his taqwa through it. This serves as an explanation of the muttaqi (God-fearing), because the muttaqi is the one who guards against shirk and ta'til (denial of God's attributes), does not deny Him, and does not acknowledge anything other than Him; the awwab is the one who does not acknowledge anything other than Him and turns back from everything other than God the Exalted; and the hafiz is the one who has not turned back from Him to anything else among what is apart from Him.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever feared the Most Merciful unseen and came with a penitent heart﴾. There are several views concerning "man" (*man*):

The first, which is the strangest of them, is that it is a vocative (*munada*), as if He, exalted is He, said: "O you who feared the Most Merciful, enter it in peace." The omission of the vocative particle is common.

The second is that "man" is a substitute (*badal*) for "kull" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for every penitent﴾, without repeating the preposition. Its implied meaning is: "The Garden has been brought near for whoever feared the Most Merciful unseen."

The third concerns His saying, exalted is He: ﴿penitent, guardian﴾. It is a known, unmentioned described noun, as if He says: "for every person who is penitent, or a servant, or other than that." So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿whoever feared the Most Merciful unseen﴾ is a substitute for that described noun.

These are three views which al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) mentioned, and he said: "It is not permissible for it to be a substitute for 'penitent' or 'guardian,' because 'penitent' and 'guardian' have been described by a known, unmentioned described noun, as we have explained. A substitute has the ruling of the thing substituted for. So 'man' would be described by them, and 'man' cannot be described by them. One does not say: 'The man *man* came to me sat with me,' as one says: 'The man *alladhi* came to me sat with me.'" This is the complete statement of al-Zamakhshari. If someone says: "If *man* and *alladhi* share being relative pronouns (*mawsulat*), why do they not share the permissibility of being described by them?" We say: The matter is intelligible, and we will explain it with regard to *ma*, and from it the matter with regard to it becomes clear. We say: *ma* is an ambiguous noun that applies to everything, so its concept is "a thing" (*shay'*). But "thing" is the most general of things: substance is a thing, accident is a thing, the Necessary Being is a thing, the contingent is a thing, and so on. The more general is prior to the more specific in understanding, because when you see a shape from afar you first say, "It is a thing." Then when some feature specific to people appears to you, you say, "A human." When it becomes clear that it is male, you say, "It is a man." When you find it to be strong, you say, "A brave one," and so on. So the more general is more known, and it is prior to the more specific in understanding. The concept of *ma* is thus prior to everything, so it cannot be a description, because a description comes after the described. This is from the rational standpoint. As for the grammatical standpoint, realities (*haqa'iq*) are not described by them. One does not say: "A body, a man, came to me," as one says: "A body, a speaking one, came to me," because a description subsists in the described, whereas a reality subsists in itself, not in another. Everything that functions as a description of another has as its meaning "a thing that has such-and-such." So our saying "knowing" (*'alim*) means "a thing that has knowledge" or "knowingness," and the concept of the description thus includes "a thing" together with another matter, namely "having such-and-such." But for a mere "thing" there is nothing in it that completes the description, which is the other matter whose meaning is "possessing such-and-such." So it was not permissible for it to be a description. Once this is clear, *man* for rational beings is like *ma* for other beings, and among them *man* means "a human" or "an angel" or other rational realities. Realities are not used as descriptions. As for that which applies to realities and to attributes, and whose concept includes more definition than what is included in the figurative use of *ma* rather than *man*...

And in the verse there are subtle semantic points:

The first: *al-khashya* (awe-fear) and *al-khawf* (fear) have the same meaning according to the lexicographers, but there is a difference between them: *khashya* arises from the greatness of the one feared, because the letters *kh-sh-y* in their permutations entail the sense of awe. It is said: "*shaykh*" for a lord and for an old man, and both are venerable. *Khawf* is fear arising from the weakness of the one who fears, because the letters *kh-w-f* in their permutations indicate weakness, as the words *al-kheefa* and *al-khufya* (stealth) indicate. And were it not for the closeness of their meanings, the Qur'an would not have included ﴿humbly and secretly﴾ [Al-An'am: 63] and ﴿humbly and with fear﴾. The one who is hidden (*al-makhfi*) in it has weakness, like the one who fears. When you know this, the subtle point becomes clear to you, which is that God, exalted is He, in many places mentioned the word *khashya* where the fear arises from the greatness of the one feared. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ [Fatir: 28], and He said: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from fear of God﴾ [Al-Hashr: 21]. For the mountain has no weakness for which fear would arise from its weakness; rather God is great, and every strong being fears Him. And ﴿they who fear their Lord with reverence﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 57], even though the angels are strong. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and you feared the people, while God has more right that you should fear Him﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 37], i.e., you feared them out of reverence for them, since there is no weakness in you relative to them. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 33], i.e., do not fear out of weakness, for they have no greatness. And He said: ﴿they fear a Day﴾ [Al-Nur: 37], where the greatness of the Day compared to the greatness of God is weak. And He said: ﴿that you should not fear and should not grieve﴾ [Fussilat: 30], i.e., because of an unpleasant thing that would befall you from the Hereafter, for all unpleasant things are repelled from you. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿fearful, watching﴾ [Al-Qasas: 21], and He said: ﴿I fear that they will kill me﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 14], because of his loneliness and weakness. And Aaron said: (Indeed I feared) [Ta-Ha: 94], because of Moses' greatness in Aaron's eyes, not because of any weakness in him. And He said: ﴿so we feared that he would burden them with transgression and disbelief﴾ [Al-Kahf: 80], where there was no weakness in Him. The sum of the matter is that when you reflect on the usage of *khashya*, you find it used for fear because of the greatness of the one feared. And when you look at the usage of *khawf*, you find it used for awe arising from the weakness of the one who fears. This holds for most cases, and the claim may sometimes not apply, but the majority is sufficient.

The second: God, exalted is He, said here: ﴿feared the Most Merciful﴾, even though the attribute of mercy usually opposes awe, as an indication of praising the God-fearing one, since mercy did not prevent him from fear because of greatness. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from fear of God﴾ [Al-Hashr: 21], as an indication of condemning the disbeliever, since the divinity indicated by the word *Allah*, in which is greatness, did not move him to fear. And He said: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ [Fatir: 28], because *innama* (only) is restrictive, so it indicates that the ignorant one does not fear Him. He mentioned *Allah* to show that the non-fear of Him, despite the existence of the motive and the absence of an obstacle (which is mercy), is itself the issue. We have mentioned this in Surat Ya-Sin, and we add here something else: the word *al-Rahman* indicates a motive, not an obstacle. The Most Merciful (*al-Rahman*) means the giver of existence through creation, and the Merciful (*al-Rahim*) means the giver of continuance through provision. He is in this world *Rahman*, since He brought us into being out of mercy, and *Rahim*, since He sustains us with provision. And it is not said of anyone else that he is *Rahim*, because continuance through provision may be thought to come likewise from one who feeds the destitute, so one says: "So-and-so is the one who sustained so-and-so." In the Hereafter also He is *Rahman*, since He brings us into being again, and *Rahim*, since He provides for us. We have mentioned this in the commentary on the Opening (al-Fatiha), where we said: ("In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Merciful") indicates that He is Merciful (*Rahman*) in this world in creating us, and Merciful (*Rahim*) in this world in providing for us. Then He said again after His saying: ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, ﴿the Most Merciful, the Merciful﴾ [Al-Fatiha: 2-3], i.e., He is *Rahman* once more in the Hereafter by creating us a second time. We derived this from His saying after that: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ [Al-Fatiha: 4], i.e., He recreates us, and He is *Rahim*, providing for us and being the Master on that Day. When you know this, the one from whom a human's existence comes, his fear should be fear of Him and not of another. For the speaker says to another: "I fear that you will cut off my provision or change my life." So when God, exalted is He, is the *Rahman* from whom existence comes, He should be feared, for the one in whose hand is existence is in whose hand is non-existence. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The fear of God is the head of all wisdom." This is because the wise person, when he reflects on other than God, finds it subject to change and liable to non-existence at every moment of an eye's blink. And perhaps God decrees its non-existence before it can cause harm, because if God does not decree that something harm, it has no power to harm. And if it has power to harm by God's decree, the harm will cease with the death of the one tormented or the tormentor. But as for God, exalted is He, there is no repeller of what He wills, and no end to His punishment. He, exalted is He, said: (unseen), i.e., their fear was before the matters became manifest as seen with the eye. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and came with a penitent heart﴾ indicates another attribute of praise. This is because the one who fears may flee and abandon nearness to the one feared and gain nothing. But when the one feared knows that he is under God's command, he knows that fleeing will not benefit him, so he comes to the one feared while not fleeing, as the runaway slave flees. So He said: (and came), and did not go away as the runaway goes. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with a penitent heart﴾: the particle *bi* (with) here may have several meanings, which we mentioned in His saying: ﴿and the agony of death came with truth﴾ [Qaf: 19].

First: the transitive sense, i.e., he brought a sound heart, just as one says "he took it away" when he caused it to go away.

Second: accompaniment, as one says: "So-and-so bought the horse with its saddle," i.e., together with its saddle, and "So-and-so came with his family," i.e., together with his family.

Third, which is the best known: *bi* of causation. One says: "So-and-so took only by the word of so-and-so, and came with a plea to him." So it is as if He said: he came, and did not come except because of a penitence in his heart, knowing that there is no return except to God, so he came because of his penitent heart. The penitent heart is like the sound heart in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾ [Al-Saffat: 84], i.e., sound from polytheism. Whoever is sound from polytheism leaves other than God and returns to God, so he is penitent. And whoever turns in penitence to God is free from polytheism, so he is sound.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Enter it in peace.﴾

The pronoun refers to the Garden mentioned in ﴿And the Garden will be brought near﴾, meaning: when its beauty and nearness were complete, and it was said to them that it is their abode by His saying: ﴿This is what you were promised﴾, they were given permission to enter it. In this there are several issues.

The first issue: To whom is the address directed? We say: if it is read "ما تُوعَدُونَ" with the letter ta' (you, plural addressed), then it is clear, since there is no doubt that the address is to those who were promised. If it is read with the letter ya' (they), then the address is to the God-fearing, meaning it is said to the God-fearing: "Enter it."

The second issue: This indicates that entry depends on permission, and there is in this a waiting that does not befit honor. We say: it is not so. For whoever invites an honored guest to his orchard opens the gate for him and sits in his place, and does not stand at the gate waiting for someone to welcome him, and says: "When you reach my orchard, enter it." And if there is no one there, he has not neglected his honoring. This is unlike one who stands at the gate of a people who say: "Enter in the name of God." The indication of honor is His saying, exalted is He: (in peace), as the host says: "Enter accompanied by safety, happiness and honor." The "bi" (ب) here denotes accompaniment, in the sense of a state (ḥāl), meaning: safe, joined with safety. Or its meaning is: enter it, greeted; and God and His angels greet you. In my view there is another possibility: that this is a guidance for the believers toward noble manners on that day, just as they were guided to them in this world, where He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your own until you seek permission and greet their occupants﴾ [al-Nur: 27]. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: This is your home and your abode, but do not abandon your good customs, and do not neglect your noble manners; so enter it in peace. And they will cry out "Peace" upon those within it, and those within it will greet them, and they will say: "Peace be upon you." This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 26], meaning they greet those within it, and those within it greet them. This view, if it is transmitted, then good; and if it is not transmitted, then it is rationally fitting, and it is supported by a transmitted proof.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is the Day of Eternity﴾.

Lest it enter their hearts that this might end for them, and the regret of it remain in their hearts. If it is said: the believer already knows that when he enters Paradise he will abide in it forever, so what is the benefit of the reminder? The answer to this is from two aspects.

One of them: His saying ﴿That is the Day of Eternity﴾ is a statement God made in this world as information and report, and it is not a statement He makes at the time of His saying "Enter it." So it is as if He, exalted is He, informed us, in our world, that this day is ﴿the Day of Eternity﴾.

The second: assurance of the heart is greater by speech. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding His saying ﴿the Day of Eternity﴾: it is an ellipsis, its estimate being: "That is the day of the decree of eternity." It may also be said that "yawm" (day) is used while meaning absolute time, whether it is a day or a night. We say: "The day a son is born to so-and-so," there is great joy, and if he had been born to him at night, the joy would still be attained; so you mean by it time. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: That is a time of permanent abode.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿For them is whatever they wish therein, and with Us is more.﴾

In the verse there is an arrangement of utmost beauty, because He, exalted is He, began by explaining their honor, saying: ﴿And the Garden will be brought near for the God-fearing﴾, and He did not say: "The God-fearing will be brought near to the Garden," as an explanation of honor, in that He made them among those to whom the gardens are conveyed with what is in them of beauties. Then He explained that it is the reward of their righteous deeds by His saying: ﴿for every penitent, keeper [of covenant]﴾, His saying: ﴿who feared the Most Merciful﴾. For the disposal of an owner who possesses something in exchange (for payment) is more complete than the disposal of one who possesses without exchange, since it is possible to retract a gift without exchange. Then He increased the honor by His saying: "Enter it," as we have explained, that this is honor; for whoever opens his door to people, and there is no one at his door to welcome those entering, has not yet given complete honor. Then He said: ﴿That is the Day of Eternity﴾, meaning: do not fear what befell you before, when He caused your two parents to leave it; for this is an entry after which there is no exit from it.

Then, when He explained that they (abide therein forever), He said: Do not fear the cessation of your provisions and that you will remain in need, as you were in the world, where whoever lived long was made to decline and became needy. Rather, for you is eternity, and what you enjoy will not run out. So for you is whatever you wish, at whatever time you wish. And to God is the final end; and upon reaching Him and standing before Him, what is with Him cannot be described, and no one can know it, and the greatness of Him who is with Him points you to the excellence of what is with Him. This is the arrangement. As for the exegesis, there are two issues:

The second: that it is a matter of shifting (iltifāt), and the wisdom is combining the two sides, as if He, exalted is He, says: He honored them with it in their presence; so in their presence there is joy, and in their absence there are the maidens and the palaces.

As for Me, with Me is what does not occur to their minds, and you cannot attain to it.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿How many generations did We destroy before them, who were mightier in strength than they?﴾

When He had warned them of the great Day and the painful punishment that lies ahead of them, He warned them of the destroying punishment that would be hastened upon them and of the overtaking destruction, and He explained to them the condition of those who came before them. Its interpretation (tafsir) has already been given in several places, but the matters specific to this passage are as follows:

First: If this was to combine the warning of the hastened punishment with the deferred retribution, why did the words of the Exalted come between the two: ﴿And Paradise is brought near to the God-fearing﴾ up to His words: ﴿And with Us is more﴾? We say: so that this would be a call to both fear and hope. Then the Exalted said: If you are in doubt about the everlasting, endless punishment, then you are not in doubt about the hastened, destroying punishment that destroyed those like you. If it is said: why did He not combine warning and encouragement in the present life as He combined them in the next life, and why did He not mention the condition of those who submitted before and were blessed, as He mentioned the condition of those who associated partners with Him and so were destroyed? We say: because blessing had already reached them, and they were moving about in blessings, so He did not remind them of it. They were only heedless of destruction, so He warned them of it. As for the Hereafter, they were heedless of both matters together, so He informed them of both.

Second: His words: ﴿So they roamed through the lands﴾.

Regarding its meaning there are several views:

One: it is what He said concerning Thamud: ﴿who hewed out the rocks in the valley﴾ [al-Fajr: 9]. By their strength they tunneled through the roads and pierced them, and they cut through the rocks and bored into them.

Two: "naqqabu" means they travelled in journeys and found no refuge or place of escape. On this view, it may be that the intended people are the people of Makkah, i.e., they traveled in journeys and saw the traces that remained in them.

Three: ﴿So they roamed through the lands﴾ means they became "nuqaba'" (leaders/chieftains) over the earth, that is, what their might and strength gave them. This is indicated by the fa' (the "so"), because in this case it indicates the consequence of the matter following from its cause. You say: Zayd was stronger than 'Amr, so he overcame him; 'Amr was sick, so Zayd overcame him. Likewise here, He said: ﴿they were mightier in strength than them﴾, so they became chieftains in the land. It was also read as ﴿fa-naqqabu﴾ with the doubled letter (tashdid), and this too indicates what we mentioned in the third view, because "tanqib" is searching, and it is from "naqaba" in the sense of becoming a "naqib" (chief).

Third: His words: ﴿Is there any escape?﴾.

It admits three possibilities:

The first: according to the reading of the one who read with the tashdid, it may be said that it is an object (maf'ul), i.e., they searched for an escape: ﴿Is there any escape?﴾.

The second: according to all the readings, it is an interrogative in the sense of denial, i.e., there was no escape for them.

The third: it is a resumed statement, as if the Exalted were saying to the people of Muhammad (ﷺ): they were destroyed despite the strength of their might: ﴿Is there any escape?﴾ for you, on which you may rely? The "mahis" is like the "mahid" (place of avoidance), except that "al-mahis" is a deviation and a flight away from hardship. This is shown by their saying: "they fell into haysa bayss", i.e., into hardship and constriction. And "al-mahid" is a deviation, even though it may be by choice; it is said: "hada 'an al-tariq nazaran" (he swerved from the road by looking), but it is not said: "hasa 'an al-amr nazaran".

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us.﴾ He repeated the proof a second time. We have already explained this in the commentary on Surat al-Sajda, and we said that bodies are of three kinds.

The first of them is the heavens. Then He set them in motion and specified them with attributes and positions. Likewise, He created the earth, then spread it out (dahaha). Likewise, He created what is between them, their individual kinds and categories. ﴿In six days﴾ is an indication of six stages (atwar). What shows this and establishes it is that the meaning of "days" cannot be the concept as understood in the linguistic usage (wad' al-lugha), because "yawm" (day) in the language denotes the period during which the sun stays above the earth from sunrise to sunset, and before the creation of the heavens there was no sun or moon. But "yawm" is also used to mean a period of time. One says, "The day a son is born to the king there will be great joy," and "the day so-and-so dies there will be intense grief," even if the birth or death happened at night. This is not restricted to the day, and it falls within the intent of the speaker, because he meant by "day" merely a time and a period. Once you know this state of affairs regarding the attribution of "day" to actions, understand what is meant by the unrestricted use of "day" in His words: ﴿six days﴾.

Some exegetes said: the intent of the verse is a refutation of the Jews, who said that God, exalted is He, began the creation of the world on Sunday, finished it in six days, the last of which was Friday, rested on Saturday, and reclined upon His Throne. So God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And no weariness touched Us﴾ as a refutation of them. The apparent meaning is that the intent is a refutation of the polytheist, and an argument from the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. His words, exalted is He: ﴿And no weariness touched Us﴾ mean: We did not become weary in the first creation so as to be unable to repeat it.

Second: the new creation, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Were We wearied by the first creation?﴾ [Qaf: 15]. As for what the Jews said and transmitted from the Torah, it is either a distortion on their part or they did not know its interpretation. That is because Sunday and Monday are times distinguished from one another. So if the creation of the heavens had begun on Sunday, time would have been established before bodies, and time does not separate from bodies, so there would be other bodies before the creation of bodies, which entails the claim that the world is eternal (qidam al-'alam), and that is the doctrine of the philosophers (falasifa). It is strange that between the philosophers and the Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists) there is the utmost disagreement. The philosopher does not affirm any attribute for God, exalted is He, at all, and says that God, exalted is He, does not receive an attribute; rather He is one in every respect, so His knowledge, His power, and His life are His reality, His essence, and His self. The anthropomorphist affirms for God the attributes of bodies, such as motion and rest, istiwa' (settling), sitting, ascending, and descending, so there is a contradiction between them. Then the Jews, in this statement, combined the two questions: they took the doctrine of the philosophers on the question most particular to them, which is eternity, since they affirmed before the creation of bodies countable days and limited times, and they took the doctrine of the anthropomorphists on the question most particular to them, which is istiwa' upon the Throne. Thus they erred [and went astray] and led others astray regarding both time and place.

So His saying, ﴿and after the prostrations﴾, that is, following what you have prostrated and worshipped, declare your Lord free with proof at the gathering of the people, so that worship through prostration and guidance may both be attained for you, "after the prostrations."

The third: that the intended meaning is "Say: Glory be to God." This is because a number of words have come to mean uttering their speech. Our saying "kabbara" is used to mean the speaker's saying "Allahu akbar"; "sallama" is used to mean his saying "as-salamu 'alaykum"; "hamdala" is said of one who says "al-hamdu lillah"; "hallala" is said of one who says "la ilaha illa Allah"; and "sabbaha" is said of one who says "subhan Allah." So if one were to say, "So-and-so said, 'There is no god but God,' or said, 'God is greatest,'" the speech would be lengthened, and so the need arose for a single word that conveys this, because what came first is not repeated. As for the relevance of this meaning to the passage in which it occurs: their denial of the Messenger, their wonder at his words, or their mockery would ordinarily require the Prophet ﷺ to occupy himself with cursing them, reviling them, and invoking curses against them. So He said: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾, and make your speech, instead of invoking curses upon them, the glorification of God and praise of Him. Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And listen, on the day the caller calls from a near place.﴾

This indicates the explanation of the goal of glorifying (tasbih): that is, occupy yourself with glorifying God and await the caller, as in His saying, exalted: ﴿And worship your Lord until certainty (yaqin) comes to you﴾ [al-Hijr: 99]. And concerning it there are issues:

The first issue: What is it that he listens to? We say: it admits three possibilities.

The first: that its object is left out entirely, and the intended meaning is "Be a listener, and do not be like those heedless, disregarding ones." It is said: "He is a listening, obedient man," and no specific thing heard is intended, just as one says "So-and-so is a cup-bearer" or "So-and-so gives and withholds."

The second: "Listen to what is revealed to you."

The third: "He listened to the call of the caller."

The second issue: The phrase ﴿the day the caller calls﴾ is in the accusative by which verb? We say: it is based on the first issue. If we say "listen" has no object, then its governing element is what is indicated by His saying, exalted: ﴿That is the day of coming forth﴾ [Qaf: 42]; its implied meaning is: they will come forth on the day the caller calls. If we say its object is "what is revealed," then its implied meaning is: ﴿And listen﴾ to what is revealed ﴿on the day the caller calls﴾. The above also allows another possibility: "what is revealed," meaning: what is revealed ﴿on the day the caller calls﴾, hear it. If it is objected that "listen" is coordinated with "so be patient" and "glorify," and those are in this world, and listening occurs in this world, whereas what is revealed on the day the caller calls is not listened to in this world, we say: this is not necessary, because it may be said "pray and enter Paradise," meaning pray in this world and enter Paradise in the next. Likewise here. It may also be said that "listen" means "await," so gathering can be in this world. And if we say "listen to the Blast," which is the caller's call: "O bones, disperse!" then the question raised is answered by it. There is another answer we give at that point, namely that God, exalted, said: ﴿And the Trumpet is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth swoons, except whom God wills﴾ [az-Zumar: 68]. We say: those whom God wills are those who knew the occurrence of the Blast and awoke to it, so it did not alarm them, like one who sees a flash of lightning and knows that after it there will be a strong thunderclap, so he looks at it and listens for it, while another is heedless; when the thunder crashes with force, it may overcome the heedless one, while the listener is not affected by it. So He said: "(Listen)," that you may not be among those who swoon on that day.

The second issue (continued): Who is the one who calls the caller? There are possible views, transmitted and rationally grounded, and their enumeration is that we say: the caller is either God, exalted, or the angels, or others; and those addressed among humankind and jinn are the ones obligated outwardly, and others do not call. If we say it is God, exalted, there are views:

The first: He calls: ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their spouses﴾ [as-Saffat: 22].

The second: He calls: ﴿Cast into Hell every stubborn disbeliever﴾ [Qaf: 24], along with His saying: ﴿Enter it in peace﴾. Similar is His saying, exalted: ﴿Seize him and shackle him﴾ [al-Haqqah: 30]. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿on the day the caller calls from a near place﴾, and He said: ﴿And they will be seized from a near place﴾ [Saba': 51].

The third: others than these two, according to His saying: ﴿He will call to them: "Where are My partners?"﴾ [Fussilat: 47], and other than that.

As for our view that the caller is other than God, there are also views on it.

The first: the saying of Israfil: "O decayed bones, gather for the reunion and listen to the decision."

The second: the call directed at the soul: it is said to the soul, ﴿Return to your Lord﴾ [al-Fajr: 28], to enter your place in Paradise or the Fire.

The third: a caller calls: "These to Paradise and those to the Fire," as He, exalted, said: ﴿A party in Paradise and a party in the Blaze﴾ [ash-Shura: 7].

On our view that the caller is an obligated being, it may be said that it is what God, exalted, explained in His saying: ﴿And they will call, "O Malik!"﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 77], or something other than that. As for God, exalted, being a caller, this has already occurred in this surah in His saying: ﴿Cast﴾, and this is a call; and His saying: ﴿on the day We say to Hell﴾, and this is a call. As for the obligated being, it is not like that. And His saying, exalted: ﴿from a near place﴾ is an indication that the voice is not hidden from anyone, but everyone equally hears it. On this basis, it is not far-fetched to take the caller as God, exalted, since the intended by "near place" is not the place itself but the manifestness of the call, and it is from God, exalted, that it is nearer. This is like His saying in this surah: ﴿And We are nearer to him than the jugular vein﴾, and that is not a place.

Its explanation is that He said "listen" (istami'), meaning: be alert before you listen, because of its occurrence. Listening is necessary for everyone, and you and they are equal in it. The governing element (*'amil*) for both is the verb indicated by His words ﴿That is the Day of Coming Forth﴾ [Qaf: 42], meaning: they will come forth on the day they hear.

The second: that "yawma yasma'una" (on the day they hear) is governed by what is in His words "(that)" ﴿on the day the caller calls﴾, and the governing element for it is what we mentioned.

The third: it may be said that "istami'" (listen) governs "yawma yunadi" (on the day the caller calls), as we mentioned, and "yunadi" (calls) governs "yasma'un" (they hear). That is because "yawma yunadi", although it cannot be in the accusative governed by its genitive complement, which is "yunadi", can be governed by something else. It is said: "Recall the condition of Zayd and his humiliation on the day 'Amr struck him, and on the day 'Amr was governor," when the speaker intends to show Zayd's humiliation at the time when Zayd was honoured for some reason. So "yawma kana 'Amrun waliyan" (on the day 'Amr was governor) is not in the accusative governed by "udhkur" (recall), because the speaker's purpose is to remind of Zayd's condition and humiliation, and that was on the day of the striking. Rather, "yawma kana 'Amrun" is in the accusative governed by "daraba-hu 'Amrun" (struck him, 'Amr), on the day he was governor. Likewise here He said: ﴿and listen, on the day the caller calls﴾, lest you be among those who are terrified and struck senseless. Then He explained this calling by His words ﴿the caller calls﴾, on the day ﴿they hear﴾, meaning: it will not be a hidden call such that some people do not hear it. Rather, its call will be such that its reach to one in the farthest west is like its reach to one in the east, and all of you will hear it. There is no doubt that such a sound requires that a person be prepared to hear it, and that occupies the soul with the worship and remembrance of God, exalted, and reflection upon Him. Thus a sublime benefit appears from His words: ﴿So be patient, and glorify [your Lord], and listen, on the day the caller calls, the day they hear﴾.

The *lam* in "al-Sayha" (the Cry) is for definiteness. Its condition is known, and God has mentioned it repeatedly, as in His words: ﴿It was only one Cry﴾ [Ya-Sin: 29], His words ﴿It is only one shout﴾ [al-Saffat: 19], and His words: ﴿one blast﴾ [al-Haqqah: 13].

As for His words "bi-l-haqq" (in truth), it is permissible that it be connected to "al-Sayha" (the Cry), meaning: the Cry in truth they hear. On this view there are several aspects:

The first: "al-haqq" (truth) is the Gathering (al-hashr), meaning: the Cry with the Gathering, which is true, they hear. It is said: "Zayd cried out: 'O bones, gather!'" in the manner of usage of speaking with this speech. Its implied meaning then is: they hear the Cry, "O bones, gather", and this is what is meant by "al-haqq".

The second: "al-Sayha bi-l-haqq", meaning with certainty. "Al-haqq" is certainty. It is said: "So-and-so cried out with certainty, not with conjecture or guesswork", meaning the crying out existed from him with certainty, not like an echo or other things. It functions as an adjective for "al-Sayha". It is said: "He listened with a seeking (listening)", and "he cried a cry with strength", meaning a strong cry. So it is as if He said: the Cry that is confirmed.

The third: its meaning may be the Cry accompanied by truth, which is existence. It is said: "Be, and it becomes real and exists." And it is said: "Go with safety and return with happiness", meaning accompanied and attended by. If it is said: "Explain further, for the *ba'* (bi) is in reality for attachment (ilsaq); how is the meaning of attachment understood in these places?" We say: transitivity may be achieved by *bi*. It is said: "He took Zayd away (dhahaba bi-Zaydin)", in the sense of: he attached the going to Zayd, so it came to exist as standing in him, and thus became an object. Based on our statement, the meaning is: they hear the cry of one who cries out "O bones, gather!" This is the transitivity of the verbal noun by means of *bi*. It is said: "The going of Zayd with 'Amr pleased me" (a'jabani dhahabu Zaydin bi-'Amr). Likewise His words: ﴿the Cry in truth﴾, meaning: raise the voice in accordance with the truth, which is the Gathering. He has an appointed time for it, which we will explain in another place, God willing.

The second aspect: that "al-haqq" be connected to His words ﴿they hear﴾, meaning: they hear the Cry in truth. On this there are two views:

The first: it is the saying of one who says "I heard him with certainty."

The second: the *ba'* in "yasma'una bi-l-haqq" is an oath, meaning: they hear the Cry by the true God. This is weak.

As for His words, exalted: ﴿That is the Day of Coming Forth﴾ [Qaf: 42], on it there are two views:

One of them: "dhalika" (that) is an indication to a day, meaning: that day is the Day of Coming Forth.
